t: The Role of Networks, Information, and Technology in Reducing Seismic Risk
Prosocial Behaviors: A Matter of Altruism or Public Service Motivation?
abs: In recent years, public service motivation (PSM) research has grown substantially, but is still largely limited to the field of public administration. To be able to export the theory and measures of PSM to other disciplines, we need more conceptual clarity. Some suggest PSM is analogous to altruism, whereas others warn not to confound the two concepts. Is PSM separate from altruism? How does each motivational construct relate to prosocial behaviors? We use a nationally representative panel of respondents to the Cooperative Congressional Election Study (CCES) to measure both altruism and PSM among respondents before the 2016 election and measure respondents’ participation in prosocial behaviors after the 2016 election. Using linear probability models with state fixed effects, we find that although PSM and altruism predict prosocial behaviors separately, altruism has no effect after controlling for PSM. PSM is a more consistent predictor of some prosocial behaviors than altruism, particularly in more formal contexts such as volunteering with an organization.

t: Introducing Story into Economic History and Policy
abs: Robert Shiller, 2013 Nobel laureate in Economic Sciences, recently published a book with the surprising title Narrative Economics: How Stories Go Viral and Drive Major Economic Events. The intellectual journey that took him there is a fascinating one. Always interested in forecasting, Shiller began his career as an econometrician but soon became skeptical about traditional approaches such as large-scale multiequation models and rational expectations models (Shiller 2013). In his early research, Shiller showed that actual fluctuations in stock prices were much more volatile than would be expected if investors were motivated solely by rational expectations. Subsequently, Shiller went beyond traditional economics to psychology for insight into how economic agents form their expectations and has even used investor surveys as a methodology. More willing than traditional economists to call out economic irrationality, he was one of the few who predicted the bursting of the Internet stock bubble in 2000 and the housing bubble a few years later. Shiller’s purpose in writing Narrative Economics is “to improve people’s ability to anticipate and deal with major economic events, such as depressions, recessions, or secular (that is, long-term) stagnation, by encouraging them to identify and incorporate into their thinking the economic narratives that help to define these events” (Shiller 2019, 71). He feels this is essential because “economic research has not emphasized the stories that people tell to one another and to themselves about their economic lives. … By missing the popular narratives, it also misses possibly valid explanations of major economic changes” (Shiller 2019, 276). Shiller is addressing policy-makers as well as private sector actors and therefore his work should be of interest to public administration scholars. Though Shiller cites some of the voluminous literature on narrative, his focus is on economic forecasting. The definition of narrative he starts with is distinctly casual: According to the Merriam-Webster online dictionary, a narrative is ‘a way of presenting or understanding a situation or set of events that reflects and promotes a particular point of view or set of values.’…. Narratives generally take the form of some recounting of events, whether actual or fictional, though often the specific events described are little bits of color brightening a concept and making it more contagious. (Shiller 2019, 36) Most of the book consists of Shiller’s exploration of the following nine “perennial economic narratives” in the context of both recent and distant American economic history: panic versus confidence; frugality versus conspicuous consumption; gold standard versus bimetallism (with a nod to bitcoin); labor-saving machines that replace many jobs; automation and artificial intelligence that could replace almost all jobs; real estate booms and busts; stock market bubbles; boycotts, profiteers, and evil business; and the wage-price spiral and evil labor unions. Shiller’s version of macroeconomic history is different from the traditional, which focuses on changes in key economic variables, explorations of causal mechanisms, and the decisions of policy-makers. In each chapter, Shiller presents discussions of a given narrative when it went viral, drawn from both media and other sources (books, letters, even sermons). Shiller also incorporates an analytical engine inspired by the mathematical modeling of epidemics. These models show how an epidemic at first gradually but then rapidly spreads through a population, peaks, and then recedes. His hypothesis is that when narratives go viral, awareness spreads in a similar way. Shiller takes words or phrases that express his narratives such as “automation,” “artificial intelligence,” “Great Depression,” and “American dream” and measures the frequency they appear in popular media over time. He employs Google Ngrams to show the percentage of words in all books and Proquest News and Newspaper archives to determine the percentage of all newspaper articles published in a particular year that include his chosen word or phrase. Shiller concludes his book with an ambitious research program that involves interviewing large population samples to hear their stories about their economic decisions, convening regular focus groups to discuss economic narratives, and building historical databases of focus groups’ deliberations, sermons, and personal letters and diaries that deal with economic issues. Shiller is near the end of his career, so this is a research program that his students and subsequent researchers would have to carry out. Though this research program represents a new direction for economists, it is standard practice for other disciplines such as marketing and political science. Marketers and political strategists use in-depth interviews and focus groups to enhance the effectiveness of their marketing and election campaigns. These, of course, are deeply partisan purposes. Economics, however, endeavors to serve the public good and avoid political partisanship. If, as Shiller claims, these research techniques could produce better economic policy decisions, for example, by identifying asset bubbles before they lead to painful crashes, then the question that follows is which institution should be empowered to use them. In the context of the Trump presidency, the only major economic institution that can still claim with some credibility that it is nonpartisan is the Federal Reserve. The Federal Research also has deep pockets to support research such as Shiller’s. The Federal Reserve is a research-oriented bureaucracy that is highly transparent, for example publishing detailed minutes of the Federal Open Market Committee within a month of its meetings. It has been the subject of considerable research by public administration scholars; if it began to use narratives in its decision-making, that development would elicit further public administration research. As a researcher on business and political narrative, I share with Shiller and others in our field the hypotheses that people habitually think in terms of narratives and that narratives evoke powerful emotions that impel action. I am, therefore, sympathetic with Shiller’s intent and approach. Based on my research, in particular the recent book Negotiating Business Narratives (Borins and Herst 2018), I have some suggestions. Shiller’s definition of narrative is decidedly minimalist. When Shiller discusses what he calls narratives, he is actually discussing concepts. He may include occasional events that illustrate the concept, but rarely does he outline sequences of events that would constitute a typical narrative. One of the few sequences of events he presents is that of a typical birthday party culminating in the singing of “happy birthday to you” (Shiller 2019, 97–98). Of course, that narrative is irrelevant to his theme. A second atypicality in Shiller’s economic narratives is that they rarely include individual human protagonists. Although Merriam-Webster and other definitions of narrative, such as that in Wikipedia (2019), include only events, most actual narrative texts (novels, biographies, histories, and documentary and docudrama films) include human protagonists. The reason for employing human protagonists is to provide a focus for audience identification and to facilitate their emotional experience. Consistent with the economics discipline’s focus on social forces, the protagonists in Shiller’s narratives are anonymous. The rare exceptions to Shiller’s anonymous narratives are those that involve celebrities, such as the apocryphal story he cites in which either John D. Rockefeller, Bernard Baruch, or Joseph Kennedy concluded the stock market had peaked in 1929 and decided to sell his portfolio when a shoeshine boy gave him a stock tip (Shiller 2019, 236–7). Shiller appears to attribute agency to celebrities, for example claiming, without any apparent evidence (at least to me), that “the Trump narrative epidemic contributes to the upward turn in home prices in the United States starting after 2012” (Shiller 2019, 225). If Shiller believes that this and other celebrity narratives are widely emulated by economic agents, he should focus on narratives of celebrities engaged in economic transactions (whether actual transactions or product endorsements) and attempt to measure their impact. A third issue concerns the coherence of Shiller’s narratives as a set. Shiller (2019, 15–16) recognizes efforts by literary scholars to enumerate a mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive set of basic types of plots, genres, or fables. In Negotiating Business Narratives, my coauthor and I attempted something similar, hypothesizing three axes of meaning for business narratives (the individual protagonist, the firm, and the society) and two plot trajectories (success or failure) for each axis. This generates a typology of eight business fables. We found it easy to classify over 60 narrative texts dealing with three major industries (information technology, automobile manufacturing, and financial trading) in terms of that eight-fold typology. Shiller gives no indication that he used a set of principles or concepts to derive his list of nine economic narratives, nor did he indicate whether he thinks that the list of nine includes all possible economic narratives. It would be worth his while to develop a conceptual scheme to classify economic narratives. My fourth concern is about Shiller’s use of Google Ngrams and Proquest News and Newspapers to generate his measures of the virality of economic narratives. The mathematical epidemic model that he takes as inspiration shows epidemics peaking at a substantial percentage of the population. In contrast, his economic narratives constitute less than one percent of all newspaper articles in a given year as measured by Proquest and, at most, one tenth of a percent of all words in books in a given year as measured by Google Ngrams. The mathematical model is, at best, useful in predicting the shape of the diffusion paths for Shiller’s economic narratives. It would be instructive for Shiller to search for other viral narratives that could explain the other 99% of the topics of newspaper articles. This would provide some sense of how salient economic concerns are relative to others such as war and peace, disease and health, and politics. In addition, Shiller’s focus on the virality of narratives assumes that it is the best measure of a narratives influence. The range of possible responses to a viral narrative is likely larger than either adopting or ignoring it and could include partial adoption or strategic reaction to the widespread adoption of a narrative by others.1 Perhaps the interview-based component of Shiller’s research program could shed light on such responses. Robert Shiller, eclectic economist par excellence, has delivered a thought-provoking study making the case that better understanding by policy-makers of the thinking of economic agents could lead to better macroeconomic management. One compelling instance of this would be the identification of asset bubbles and constraint of the forces creating them before they burst and create massive economic and social dislocation. Shiller has relied on ideas taken from the study of narrative to facilitate his study of the thinking of economic agents. But a deeper exploration of those ideas would only strengthen his research and advocacy.

t: Reviewers Thank You
Do Top Managers’ Individual Characteristics Affect Accounting Manipulation in the Public Sector?
abs: Drawing on upper echelons theory, the article investigates the potential impact of top managers’ background and demographic characteristics and personality traits on organizational decisions in the public sector. The top-management figure being investigated is the municipal chief financial officer (CFO) and the specific organizational decision under analysis is the extent of revenue misrepresentation during both budget formulation and execution. The empirical setting is provided by the CFOs of Italian municipalities with populations above 15,000 over a 3-year period (2012–14). Financial data are drawn from existing databases. Non-financial data are collected through an online survey. The results show that top managers’ individual characteristics and traits do influence the extent of accounting manipulation. In particular, revenue misrepresentation was found to be smaller in the presence of female managers, managers with degrees in business administration, and managers describing themselves as “conscientious”. These effects on accounting manipulation were moderated by auditors’ and opposition councilors’ oversight, managers’ experience, and the presence of local elections. The article extends upper echelons theory and its applications in several directions: from the private to the public context, from CEOs to CFOs, from managerial decisions in general to accounting choices, and from background and demographic variables to personality traits.

t: Uncooperative Federalism as Innovation
abs: Ben Merriman’s Conservative Innovators: How States are Challenging Federal Power is an incredibly timely look at the punctuated changes that have restructured American politics in recent years. In short, American federalism has changed form, and subnational (state) units have grown in policy import not because of explicit delegation from the national government but in spite of national policy prerogatives. Successful state challenges to federal authority (there are many meaty examples of this in the book ranging from formal state coordination of litigation regarding the Affordable Care Act to piecemeal state administrative strategies to shape election and immigration policy) are of course inconsistent with the Framers’ intent and with the twentieth century trends that saw the national government grow immensely in size and scope. Although the 2009–16 Obama administration and its red-state opponents represent the main temporal focus, Merriman includes a tidy epigraph-like chapter where he argues that vertical bellicosity comes from liberal states against Republican-controlled national institutions just as it had from conservative states against Obama-era national initiatives. This is reified, among other examples, by the fact that US state and local jurisdictions holding half of the US population intend to meet greenhouse gas-related promises as negotiated in the Paris Agreement after the Trump Administration loudly announced its withdrawal from the agreement (Light and Hale 2018). Merriman’s book makes two primary points that are relevant to scholars of public administration and political science. The first is that American federalism has changed to allow openings for the state–federal conflict that largely defines contemporary politics. This involves a well-structured, though not explicitly formulated, theory of opportunity structures and their determinants. This is an incredibly rich area for research and Merriman is cogent and convincing in his treatment of this process. The second contribution lies in identifying how state-level political conservatives identified these structures and innovatively exploited them for partisan and ideological gain, sometimes quite interestingly emulating liberal strategies from bygone eras. Merriman’s coverage of the recent establishment of (and judicial deference to) new state-guaranteed positive rights to, for example, secret ballots in union elections, is likely to be of great interest to legal scholars as well as to the core readership of this journal. For Merriman, the “innovation” here is not about new conservative ideological ends, but instead refers to the novel means used by these modern reformers to approach their goals. These means include a tapestry of strategies that are comprehensively described in the substantive chapters of the book. Chapter 2 traces state litigation against federal agencies (a possibility facilitated by recent Supreme Court interpretations of federal authority). Chapter 3 focuses on interstate compacts that create novel horizontal implementation structures for cross-state litigation and policy initiatives. This chapter also covers high profile “uncooperative fiscal federalism” reflected in states foregoing federal funding when they disagree with federal policy goals. Chapter 4 provides an in-depth treatment of how judicial rulings circumscribing federal power have interacted with new state administrative strategies (as well as post-Shelby County v. Holder enabled state legislation) to shape election administration in state-preferred ways. This chapter also contains an interesting secondary analysis of the racial and demographic consequences of how state election administrations function in this new era of federalism. The analysis serves as a reminder of the historical salience of federalism with respect to civil rights and is a harbinger of conflicts to come. So, how did states ultimately achieve these powers to challenge national authority, especially in policy areas, like environmental regulation and immigration, where federal prerogatives have been predominant? Merriman sets a strong foundation in chapter 1 by positing that what might seem at first glance to be revolutionary change is better understood as evolutionary adaptation driven by three concurrent and increasingly well-understood trends. First, national and state governments have experienced gradual shifts in the balance of power between executive and legislative branches. American presidents have honed their ability to use unilateral policymaking to bypass fractured Congresses; state executives (governors, agencies, attorneys general, etc.) have an additional boon in the form of resource advantages over “amateur” legislatures with weak oversight powers. The second trend is the ubiquity of party polarization, which operates distinctly across federal and state levels. Where national party competition is keen and divided government the norm, many states have more homogenous citizenries that regularly produce trifectas of unified executives and legislative chambers. The effect is often that the national policy-making process is divided, which can lead presidents to push their programs unilaterally through executive orders, memoranda, and rulemaking. By contrast, states that oppose a given president’s policy program often do so unanimously and can assert their opposition forcefully and in coordination with similar states. The final trend is in the legal means available to states to opt out of national policy when it suits their preferences. Merriman does an exceptionally good job here describing the evolution of Supreme Court doctrine from near-complete deference to the federal executive apparatus to one that is highly skeptical of executive power (especially with respect to agency rulemaking). The upshot is that national policy is tenuously crafted and ultimately susceptible to state challenges and that roughly half the nation’s states will always be in conflict with the national government. The argument about the structural determinants of this new era of what Merriman calls “uncooperative” federalism is likely to be of great interest to political scientists (the author of this review included), and, although I find the argument plausible, Merriman might have done more to firmly establish and assess this account. For example, although executives do predominate in most American governments, the extent to which they do varies quite a bit across the states (e.g., Boushey and McGrath 2017). In particular, scholars of state politics and policy will be surprised to find that Merriman does not leverage variation in legislative professionalism (Squire 2007), oversight capabilities, or ideological unanimity across states to help explain which state officials have been at the vanguard of challenging federal power. Such an examination could provide support for the explicit role of executive–legislative imbalance in creating opportunities for nonaligned (with the president) governors, attorneys general, and other actors to sue or otherwise conflict with the national government. In fact, although Merriman describes instances of state conflict with the national government, the book provides scant original data on this process and does not offer an empirical examination of whether this activity has meaningfully increased over time or correlates with the posited structural explanations. Although the account here is consistent with conventional wisdom, without specifying a theory and data generating process more specifically, skeptics might see the new federalism Merriman describes as a reflection of some process other than state innovation. For example, are state officials really the “innovative” figures here, or are they being directed by national partisan actors? Despite this weakness, Merriman’s work on this issue is sure to generate future research. Whereas this is a bit of a missed opportunity, the book’s emphasis on conservative politics and policy in Kansas (chapter 5) strikes me as a misfire, even according to Merriman’s stated goals. As mentioned, Merriman sets out to distinguish innovation in state strategies to achieve policy against an opponent national government rather than to delve into the specific ideological ends preferred by conservatives in this era. In addition, the book makes convincing arguments both that these strategic means are novel and that they are more subterranean than what the modal political science account would look for (legislative action facilitated by the American Legislative Exchange Council, for example). The Kansas chapter, while containing worthwhile detail on the specifics of that case, does not contribute much to the overall argument of the book because it focuses on politics and policymaking internal to the state and on standard policymaking procedures rather than on novel applications on the subtle policymaking described in the preceding chapters. It reads as an opportunity to examine innovation in conservative ends in a way that the rest of the book eschews. The placement of the Kansas chapter also requires Merriman to transition to the final chapter by way of a hurried discussion of historical Progressivism that also fails to contribute much. In the end, this discussion of ideological innovation and zealotry in Kansas could easily have been replaced with a more in-depth examination of state-to-state and/or temporal emulation of state executive strategies described throughout the book. Despite this critical assessment, the rest of the book holds together nicely and provides plenty of value to public administration scholars, political scientists, and legal experts. The writing is engaging yet objective, which serves to heighten the intellectual importance of the subject at hand. As Merriman recognizes in chapter 1, the current balance of federalism is just the latest in a series of swings and roundabouts in national–state relations, but its potentially negative implications regarding equity and civil rights are apparent from Merriman’s work in chapter 4, especially. In addition to its impact on the academy, I am sure that state and local political practitioners will find lessons in the book. Yet, consistent with the history that Merriman presents in Conservative Innovators, I would expect that we will soon recognize an entirely new structure of opportunities and constraints in American federalism—swings and roundabouts.

t: The Sexual Harassment of Federal Employees: Gender, Leadership Status, and Organizational Tolerance for Abuses of Power
abs: Theory and research suggest that sexual harassment is often a dominance strategy used to undermine women’s power, but the precise relationships between government employees’ workplace power, organizational climate, and vulnerability to particular types of sexual harassment remain under-specified. This study analyzes data from the 2016 US Merit Systems Protection Board survey of the federal civilian workforce (the most comprehensive and up-to-date national data on workplace sexual harassment) to test predictions about how employees’ workplace power and their agency’s efforts to mitigate abuses of power affect their likelihood of experiencing sexual harassment. Findings reveal that women in leadership positions report more sexual harassment than non-leaders, and that team leaders (i.e., those without formal supervisory authority) and executives (i.e., those with the most authority) report more sexual harassment than women in middle management. At the organizational level, sexual harassment occurs in workplaces with higher levels of non-sexual aggression and among employees who perceive their agency as less proactive in preventing and responding to social inequity. Taken together, findings suggest that sexual harassment is a dominance strategy not unlike other forms of aggression used to undermine women in power, and that workplace climates that are effective at mitigating abuses of power reduce the likelihood of experiencing sexual harassment. These results have implications for how government agencies can implement policies that not only prevent harassment but also promote democracy and equity among an increasingly diverse federal workforce.

t: Learning from Performance Information
abs: Years of research on performance management has generally concluded that performance information is seldom used purposefully by public managers and that it does not improve performance as intended. More recently, both theoretical and empirical work have begun to focus on situations in which performance management may facilitate internal organizational learning. In this study, we focus on one key component in performance management systems, namely generation of performance information. Based on a Bayesian learning model, we argue that generation of performance information at the individual level may create performance improvements because both users and frontline workers may learn where to prioritize their efforts. To test the isolated effect of this key component of any performance management system, we use as-good-as-random variation in exposure of students to testing because of a technical breakdown in an IT system. We identify the effect of testing on student learning measured two years after the breakdown. Results show positive and statistically significant effects of about 0.1 standard deviations, which is comparable to much more expensive interventions, and effects tend to persist after four years. We find larger effects for students with low socioeconomic status but also that schools with many students from this group are more reluctant to measure their performance. Implications and limitations in terms of increasing the level of student testing are discussed.

t: Why and How Does Participatory Governance Affect Policy Outcomes? Theory and Evidence from the Electric Sector
abs: In many policy arenas, decision makers have supplemented or even replaced traditional forms of bureaucratic decision making with more participatory approaches to governance. While theory suggests that participatory governance can have an instrumental effect on policy outcomes, there have been few efforts to systematically test these theories across multiple jurisdictions. This study asks whether and how participatory governance in electric sector regulation affects utilities’ energy savings. Using a mixed-methods research design, this study develops hypotheses drawn from participatory governance theory, analyzes regulatory documents to operationalize a set of participatory governance variables, and uses a multilevel fixed effects model to test whether these participatory governance variables have an effect on electricity consumption by customers of 250 utilities across 42 states between 2000 and 2015. Model results show that deliberation among stakeholders has a significant decrease in electricity use by consumers, but that this effect must be realized over time as stakeholders gain experience with the deliberative process. To explore why deliberation produces this effect, the study presents qualitative evidence from Connecticut and Maryland, two states that have used participatory governance to regulate utilities’ energy efficiency plans. Results suggest that information exchange among participants has a direct effect on utilities’ energy efficiency plans. Participatory governance also contributes to a network of engaged stakeholders who can help hold utilities accountable for achieving their savings goals.

t: Pathways to Implementation: Evidence on How Participation in Environmental Governance Impacts on Environmental Outcomes
abs: There is much enthusiasm among scholars and public administrators for participatory and collaborative modes of governance as a means to tackle contemporary environmental problems. Participatory and collaborative approaches are expected to both enhance the environmental standard of the outputs of decision-making processes and improve the implementation of these outputs. In this article, we draw on a database of 305 coded published cases of public environmental decision-making to identify key pathways via which participation fosters effective environmental governance. We develop a conceptual model of the hypothesized relationship between participation, environmental outputs, and implementation, mediated by intermediate (social) outcomes such as social learning or trust building. Testing these assumptions through structural equation modeling and exploratory factor analysis, we find a generally positive effect of participation on the environmental standard of governance outputs, in particular where communication intensity is high and where participants are delegated decision-making power. Moreover, we identify two latent variables—convergence of stakeholder perspectives and stakeholder capacity building—to mediate this relationship. Our findings point to a need for treating complex and multifaceted phenomena such as participation in a nuanced manner, and to pay attention to how particular mechanisms work to foster a range of social outcomes and to secure more environmentally effective outputs and their implementation.

t: Discretionary Authority and Prioritizing in Government Agencies
abs: Government agencies have a certain freedom to choose among different possible courses of action. This article studies agency decision making on priorities in a principal–agent framework with multiple tasks. Agency leadership has discretion over part of the agency’s budget to incentivize staff in the pickup of cases. The head is concerned not only with society’s benefits from the agency’s overall performance, but also with the organization’s public image. Based on their talent and the contracts offered by the head, staff officials choose which type of task to pursue: complex major cases with an uncertain outcome or basic minor and simple cases with a higher probability of success. We show how the size of the agency’s discretionary budget influences both the scale and type of tasks it will engage in. Small changes in the budget can cause extensive restructuring from major to minor tasks, or vice versa, causing social welfare jumps. The mechanism provides overhead authorities with some control over the priorities of supposedly independent agencies. It applies generally to government bureaus with the formal and informal discretion to choose their tasks. Antitrust authorities serve as one illustration of implications for institutional design.

t: Does Partisan Conflict Lead to Increased Bureaucratic Policymaking? Evidence from the American States
abs: Scholars of American politics debate the consequences of polarized and divided government on lawmaking but have largely neglected the impact of institutional conflict on the policy outputs of the bureaucracy. We argue that lawmaking gridlock creates opportunities and demands for governors and civil servants to pursue policy goals through rulemaking. To explore these dynamics, we draw upon a comprehensive dataset of over 150,000 proposed and adopted rules issued by US state agencies from 1994 through 2009 and compare differences in rulemaking output within states across periods of divided and unified party control. We find that policy conflict (measured by the presence of a party divided legislature) leads to a 3%–7% increase in the number of proposed and adopted rules. We then explore how variation in state powers of legislative oversight affect rulemaking, and find that these effects are concentrated in governments with weaker powers of legislative review. Our research speaks to debates in the literature regarding the nature of bureaucratic policymaking and highlights practical consequences of legislative gridlock and partisan polarization.

t: Competition and Federal Contractor Performance
abs: Contracts are increasingly used in government as a way to insert competition into public agencies and policy implementation. Competition among contractors is theorized to drive down costs, encourage innovation, and boost accountability. However, there have been few studies on whether competition actually leads to improved performance among contractors. This analysis examines nearly 25,000 federal contracts to determine how competition is related to performance. Findings indicate that competitively sourced contracts are more likely to suffer from performance problems. However, relationships between contractor and agency correlate with fewer performance problems. This suggests that competition may not be leading to the benefits that many might expect. Instead, relationships and shared experiences, along with other factors, may matter more when seeking to improve contractor performance.

t: Building Institutional Trust Through Service Experiences—Private Versus Public Provision Matter
abs: Welfare service experiences are known to shape citizens' trust in public institutions and their support of the welfare state. But, there is poor understanding of how this relationship is shaped in systems of mixed provision, that is, welfare states that use public in-house as well as contracted private providers for publically funded services. Drawing on the notion of system trust this article provides a theoretical account of how mixed-provision welfare systems condition the relationship between service experience and trust, affecting the legitimacy of the state. Utilizing a randomized vignette experiment with participants in a general citizen survey in Sweden, we investigate whether it matters for the formation of institutional trust if the welfare service is provided by a public or third-party private provider. The main result show that the spillover of trust from positive service experiences with the provider to trust in public institutions is higher in cases of public service provision. Thus, the possibility of using welfare services to build trust in the welfare system seems to be greater when public provision is used.

t: Service Professionals' Response to Volunteer Involvement in Service Production
abs: Involving volunteers in the production and delivery of public services is a core policy objective of governments around the world. While existing research on volunteer involvement in service production, for example, has focused on advantages and disadvantages of such involvement and different dimensions of volunteer involvement, little is known about service professionals' response to volunteer involvement in public service production. Integrating perspectives from multiple theories, we build a theoretical framework for understanding how and when service professionals come to see volunteers as a threat to the quality of service, the profession's privileged position and monopoly, and professionals' own work tasks and job security. Based on a central distinction between production of core and complementary tasks, we propose that volunteers come to be seen as a threat in the eyes of service professionals when volunteers solve core rather than complementary tasks. Using a survey experiment among health assistants at nursing homes, we find partial support for our argument. Health assistants are more likely to perceive volunteers as a threat to the quality of care when volunteers solve core rather than complementary tasks. The study guides research toward a more nuanced understanding of volunteer involvement in service production in public organizations.

t: Assessing the Tools of Agency Control in Rulemaking: Bending the Rules
abs: Rachel Potter’s Bending the Rules: Procedural Politicking in the Bureaucracy tackles important topics related to the role of the agency as a strategic actor during rulemaking in the United States. With a novel Regulatory Proposals Dataset, she evaluates more than 11,000 rules between 1995 and 2014 from 135 different bureaus in the 15 cabinet departments as well as 15 independent agencies. Such a careful collection of rules spanning multiple administrations and partisan changes in congressional control allows Potter to systematically assess rulemaking in the United States. She finds agencies use the intricacies of procedure to help achieve desired outcomes in rulemaking. The book proceeds by framing its argument with three theoretical chapters for each procedural tool the agency can use in rulemaking. Next, it evaluates the theoretical predictions across three empirical chapters using the Regulatory Proposals Dataset to highlight the nuanced relationship between politics and rulemaking. Potter then turns to a case study of rulemaking surrounding menu labels to provide context to the empirical results. The final chapter concludes with future thoughts for the study of rulemaking. In the theoretical chapters, Potter clearly articulates the ways in which, despite the designs developed by their political principals, federal employees have the ability to gain the upper hand in achieving the agency’s ideal policy outcome. Aside from the informational asymmetry that rewards agents over principals, agencies also have three tools at their disposal throughout rulemaking, which Bending the Rules dubs procedural politicking. First, agencies, as drafters of the rule, have the ability to make the text as accessible (or inaccessible) as they desire. Write a lengthy rule or fill a rule with complex terminology, and interested parties must make significant investments to understand the rule. Second, agencies have meetings with those that are likely to be regulated. These meetings can allow the agency to anticipate roadblocks as well as produce an initial rule that might avoid consternation for the regulated parties. With the scheduling of these meetings being discretionary, agencies have considerable control over the message surrounding rules, which they use to help usher the rule to completion. Third, the agencies, unless mandated by statute, decide when they partake in rulemaking. In other words, agencies can pick when to engage in rulemaking in accordance with the political calendar. The next three chapters of the text engage each of these considerations with evidence from the Regulatory Proposals Dataset. Turning first to writing as a tool, the length of the rule’s preamble and the complexity of the abstract are used to assess this form of procedural politicking. The argument is clear and straightforward: longer preambles and more complex abstracts make it more difficult for political overseers and relevant interest groups to engage the new rule. The main finding is the more agencies are in court, the longer the rule preamble and less readable the rule abstract. For the other two branches, the results are mixed and conditional on interest group engagement. Next, Potter demonstrates that agencies strategically use timing during the rulemaking process. First, agencies possess some, but not total, latitude in how long the comment period will be for any rule. The Regulatory Proposals Dataset shows that agencies, on average, schedule two additional days for comment when groups are supportive of the agency. Second, agencies fearing congressional oversight are more likely to schedule their rulemaking during congressional recesses. Collectively, even when agencies have limited operating room, they take advantage of that space to help achieve their policy ends. The third and final empirical chapter examines how long it takes for agencies to finalize rules, finding that additional reviews by any of the three branches extend how long it takes for an agency to complete a rule. Several robustness checks are presented that show the observed behavior of the agency constitutes a sincere delay. For example, agencies could be taking longer to make sure they write the best rule possible. It is also possible that agencies facing political opposition can sometimes take longer to get the rule “right” rather than waiting out the current administration. In other words, the collision of complicated rules and politics might naturally lead to rules taking longer with no strategic manipulation on the part of the agency. However, estimates interacting complexity with political variables revealed no such pattern. This implies that delays are not a function of complexity and politics. Like the two prior chapters, this final empirical chapter leaves the reader with considerable evidence that bureaucrats, even with limited discretion and ability to manipulate outcomes for rules, act strategically to advance the interests of the agency. In sum, the results presented reflect the complicated nature of modern rulemaking. No single tool is an agency’s go-to mechanism on every rule. But this should not be surprising. Most rules are developed and implemented with little to no fanfare. There is no need for the agency to use procedural politicking tools when a rule is not going to have interjections from elected officials or the courts. As such, there are not large substantive results to display where all rules experience the same systematic decision making by agencies. Rather, this is the case for a subset of instances in which these tools are used within the sea of rules that otherwise receive little to no attention. Aside from the important contribution of the Regulatory Proposals Dataset and the empirical results presented, Potter underscores the need to blend political science and public administration traditions. As she notes, “research on bureaucracy and rulemaking takes one of two approaches, focusing either on external actors and how they can exert political influence over an agency or internal actors and how meaningfully they deliberate when making policy decisions” (p. 7). The former characterizes the political science tradition, which looks for the role of the president or Congress in administrative action. The latter characterizes work by public administration and legal scholars who predominantly keep their research contained to the system they are evaluating. Importantly, these two different frames lead to research approaches that make the disciplines ships passing in the night rather than the rising tide to lift our collective understanding of how government functions. Presidents trade off competency and loyalty in staffing the executive branch (Edwards 2001; Lewis 2008). It stands to reason then that when policy outcomes are on the line, both politics and proper administration have a role to play in explaining how policy is developed. Both factors need to be accounted for in assessing how modern government operates. The same logic about blending politics and administration applies to nearly any space where policy is being decided. Recent work has shown the influence of politics on the careers of civil servants with clear implications for the retention of a good public workforce (Ali 2019; Bolton et al. 2016; Doherty et al. 2019; Richardson 2019). Moreover, the same sorts of ambiguity in agency life regarding personnel relocations, enforcement discretion, and prioritization of tasks should also be subject to a flavor of procedural or administrative politicking. In reading the text, I was consistently making notes of where beyond rulemaking certain theoretical claims or empirical tests would apply for students of the executive branch. Bending the Rules should serve as an excellent framework to assess the policy related outcomes produced by agencies. Returning to rulemaking, one question specifically left unanswered is the distinction (if there is one) between whether it is top careerists or political appointees in the agency who control procedural politicking tools. For example, Chapter 1 uses the birth control mandate in the Affordable Care Act to show how rulemaking set policy in an issue space where the law delegated authority to the agency. The argument for creating the rule was framed around women’s health and well-being by the agency. Evidence to buttress this claim was an op-ed by Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Kathleen Sebelius that equated the mandate for birth control provisions to those for vaccinations, cancer screenings, and wellness examinations. While the HHS Secretary was acting on behalf of the agency, her position in the agency as the president’s top appointed official tasked with enacting the president’s signature piece of legislation makes it quite unlikely that her views were anything other than a reflection of the Obama administration. So, is it the agency or the president who has control over the procedural politicking tool in this instance? Another example in Chapter 6 notes the work of the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) in updating rules for crane and derrick safety. Work on the rule began and 1998 but was not completed until 2010 when “a new and more sympathetic Democratic administration led by President Barack Obama” took office (p. 132). An Obama-era administrator even noted that the rule was not an agency priority until new Labor Secretary Hilda Solis took over. On one hand, this is clearly the agency waiting out the Bush administration to eventually get a rule over the finish line. On the other hand, it certainly seems that the Bush administration was able to stop a rule when it so desired. That is strong executive influence that no amount of agency procedural politicking could overcome. Finally, an example from the Bush administration regarding No Child Left Behind (NCLB) rulemaking again notes the need to disentangle appointee steering of rulemaking from being in service of the administration or being in service of the agency. Potter notes how the rule regarding modified test taking for students with disabilities, the “two percent” rule (the percent of students school districts were authorized to give different tests to), bore no mention of this threshold in the written abstract. She argues that this was done not out of sloppiness but to obfuscate interest groups and congressional staffers looking to key in on a particularly unpopular part of the rule. Yet NCLB represents a critical domestic policy success of the Bush administration. Once clearing the legislative hurdle, it is hard to imagine the administration being hands off in crafting the rules that would ultimately shape policy implementation. So, were these writing decisions done in isolation from the executive branch by career civil servants who wanted to faithfully implement new legislation championed by the current administration? Or rather, did appointees, working in concert with careerists, craft this language to thwart congressional and interest group intervention? Regardless of which path got us to the opaque rule, it is procedural politicking. Agency discretion was used to influence the policy outcome. It just happens that understanding who is playing politics, the president or the agency, has very different implications for who has power over this procedural politicking tool. Considering these three examples and others in the book collectively, another research item for scholars to capitalize on centers on distinguishing the loyalties of appointees. Is it the case—particularly in our polarized times—that appointees, who serve at the pleasure of the president, only serve the president? Or are appointed officials placed in an agency presumably because of their political loyalty and subject matter expertise, wearing different administrative and political hats depending on the context of the situation in which they are operating? Answering these questions is critical for understanding who controls politicking tools. Bending the Rules provides an excellent summary of rulemaking in the United States. Scholars looking to understand the intricacies and long-term trends in the process will find the empirical chapters to be very valuable. Yet it is not necessary to have an intimate knowledge of rulemaking to understand the empirical results. Someone with only a passing interest in American politics (say an undergraduate political science major) will find the theoretical chapters quite accessible. This is not too surprising. Agencies wanting to have their rules read by the public make the texts of those rules accessible. Sharing this same goal with her book, Potter has crafted a very readable text for scholars and students of both public administration and political science.

t: When the Red Tape Becomes Policy: A Critical Assessment of Administrative Burdens
abs: Time-consuming procedures. Redundant information requests. Complicated forms written in an inaccessible language. Unclear responsibilities. Seemingly arbitrary requirements. In their book Administrative Burden: Policymaking by Other Means, Pamela Herd and Donald P. Moynihan trace the origins of onerous bureaucratic encounters and demonstrate how they affect citizens. They use the term “administrative burden” to describe a variety of costs that arise from interactions between citizens and the state, including tangible costs like administrative fees as well as intangible costs such as the experienced decrease in power and status. At the outset, the authors detail their personal and academic motivations for investigating burdens in the domain of social policy and foreshadow the core themes of the book. The basic assumption in the introduction, and convincingly illustrated throughout the following 10 chapters, is that administrative burdens are consequential (they restrict access to public goods), distributive (less advantaged groups face higher burdens), and constructed (burdens act as substitutes to overt policies). By exposing ideological origins of administrative burdens, Herd and Moynihan unmask them as policymaking by other means. Their conclusion constitutes a plea for minimizing the burdens imposed on citizens and for shifting burdens to the state instead. This gives the book a normative tone in the tradition of critical scholarship, though without adopting a respective paradigmatic approach. Chapter 1 details Herd and Moynihan’s conceptualization of administrative burdens. Accordingly, they consist of learning costs for gathering information about public services (e.g., programs, eligibility, points of access), compliance costs for following administrative rules (e.g., filling out forms, meeting deadlines), and psychological costs related to the stigma that arises from bureaucratic encounters (e.g., exposure of sensitive personal information, waiting in line with other beneficiaries). This three-fold definition recognizes insights from social psychology and is thus more comprehensive than traditional economic approaches to the costs of government regulations. The authors are certainly right when they assert that shifting administrative burden away from citizens depends on political will and administrative capacities. While the latter is primarily a question of resource availability, the former seems more difficult to establish. As Herd and Moynihan argue, the three qualities of burdens—opacity, controllability, and neutrality—makes them susceptible to partisan interventions disguised as technical adjustments to administrative procedures. Chapters 2–9 present in-depth case analyses of administrative burdens in the United States. The examples include voting and abortion regulations, the Affordable Care Act, Medicare, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), Medicaid in Wisconsin, the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC), and Social Security. The authors convincingly show how these policies are subject to decisions in the government’s executive branch that seek to expand or to restrict citizens’ access to benefits and fundamental rights, regardless of legislative prescriptions. Of the eight cases examined, Herd and Moynihan identify the worst burdens in voting and abortion regulations. They detail how the prevention of fraud serves as an argument to make participation in elections more burdensome, which disproportionally affects particular ethnic and social groups of American citizens. They also show how administrative requirements impose costs on patients (e.g., mandatory wait times, consultation) and treatment facilities (e.g. restrictive licensing), increasing the strain on women who are already in a difficult situation. Herd and Moynihan also deal with the continuous debate about the burdens placed on the access to health care services. Given the current state of Medicare and the Affordable Care Act, Herd and Moynihan especially criticize high information costs. They suggest simplifying the options across numerous insurance plans offered by public and private providers and expanding assistance for navigating the system’s complexities through additional hotlines and online portals. The lobbying of insurance companies against such clarity is an important point raised by the authors as it vividly illustrates the complex web of interests involved in the creation of administrative burdens. The book also includes cases in which bipartisan policies and administrative professionalism led to a considerable reduction of administrative burden for citizens. The authors use the EITC as an example for reconciling opposing political agendas. By subsidizing the low-wage sector, the program benefits both employers and the working poor. Herd and Moynihan argue that frequent reminders, the use of existing data on individual income, and an overall positive framing of the program help to reduce information, compliance, and psychological costs, respectively. The last case presents social security as a successful model for shifting burdens to the state, as evidenced by the high participation rate of 98 percent of eligible citizens. The simple requirements for participation and a well-equipped administration add to the low psychological costs of receiving benefits from a longstanding program. In both cases, Democrats and Republicans have worked together and designed administrative processes with minimal administrative burden, underscoring the book’s argument that burdens are constructed. Herd and Moynihan conclude their book by outlining an evidence-based approach to administrative burden. Following the example of business regulations, they advocate for the use of cost-benefit analyses for assessing the administration of social policy. They offer a set of “diagnostic questions about administrative burdens” (p. 258) for an estimation of learning, compliance, and psychological costs in citizen–state interactions. Although the questions do not represent validated items for the assessment of burdens, they offer an excellent starting point for a respective research agenda moving forward. Herd and Moynihan should be especially commended for considering variations in participation or take-up rates across populations. As I understand their diagnostic questions, the distributive aspect of administrative burdens serves as an “objective” characteristic for determining the effectiveness of social policies. Notwithstanding these merits, the analytic framework may benefit from further contextualization. The overall picture that Herd and Moynihan draw is that administrative burdens can and therefore should be reduced to ensure easy and equal access to public goods. The authors advocate automatic enrollment or presumptive eligibility as the gold standard for shifting burdens away from citizens. While they are generally optimistic about the positive effects of such a reform agenda, the extent to which inequalities can be traced back to distributive aspects of administrative burdens remains an empirical question. For instance, participation of less advantaged groups in German elections is lower than that of the rest of the population despite lower administrative burdens as compared to the United States (e.g., no preregistration requirements). This difference accounts for about 20% of the unemployed population and about 10% of the lowest income bracket. Thus, other factors, like political literacy or the issues on the political agenda, may account for much of the variation in voting behavior across social groups. A cost-benefit analysis should therefore identify specific boundary conditions including the conditions under which a reduction of administrative burden does not increase participation or take-up rates any further. Related to this point, the interrelationships among the three dimensions of costs as well as the linkages between these dimensions and the opportunity cost of zero burden should be considered in more detail. Much of the novelty in the authors’ approach to administrative burden lies in the acknowledgement of psychological costs. The reduction of stigma is a goal, with which I presume, (almost) everyone generally agrees. However, there are bureaucratic encounters in which a certain degree of learning and compliance costs may be a means necessary to achieve this end. Take, for example, the case of abortion. Some might argue that mandatory psychological counseling can prevent uninformed decisions or choices taken under pressure from a third party (e.g., the child’s father, family members, employers) which may result in even higher psychological costs. As a person who will never face what Herd and Moynihan describe, it is not my place to evaluate the ethical issues involved here. My point is that there are circumstances that might require a more differentiated view on the costs of administrative burdens. Administrative Burden: Policymaking by Other Means is a brilliantly written and thought-provoking book that should be situated in the context of the general debate over the scope of social policy in democratic societies. Yet despite (or maybe because of?) the book’s intended normative stance, the authors pay little attention to competing values. For instance, Herd and Moynihan strongly advocate for the use of information technology to facilitate the exchange of personal information between agencies. Although the digitalization of public administration has much potential to reduce administrative burdens for citizens, there is a thin line between unrestricted access to data for assisting citizens in precarious situations and a violation of the personal right to informational self-determination. Which undermines people’s trust in government more? Similarly, Herd and Moynihan suggest looking for “other ways of deterring fraud, or even increasing our tolerance of fraud” (p. 12). Given the potential for scandal, the question remains of how much fraud is tolerable in exchange for higher take-up rates by eligible citizens. A major challenge for Herd and Moynihan’s evidence-based approach to administrative burdens is to find “objective” measures for such competing values. So far, I gather, it depends on an individual’s perspective regarding which amount of burden is acceptable to ensure certain values and which is not. This reminds me of a similar dilemma in red tape theory in which “one man’s red tape is another man’s system” (Waldo 1946, 399). While the authors provide much evidence for a pessimistic view of the current state of public institutions in the United States, there are situations in which the consequences of administrative burdens are good. One example is the official requirements for acquiring a pilot’s license. Few would argue that learning and compliance costs should be reduced to zero in this case. Instead, the burden ensures that only those who are willing and capable to meet the requirements are selected for controlling an airplane. The authors briefly discuss a similar argument when reviewing the economic literature in Chapter 2 and indicate gun control as possible case, but they do not include a respective case study. The focus on bureaucratic encounters from the field of social policy in which, according to Herd and Moynihan, “the value of burdens seems at best debatable and at worse entirely unjustified” (p. 13), therefore obscures the limited generalizability of the book’s central claim for other citizen–state interactions. Admittedly, the authors did not set out to investigate administrative burdens in all fields of policy. Instead, they chose a critical-investigative approach and purposefully selected cases to reveal the hidden politics that shift administrative burdens to citizens. The discussion of partisan interventions is insightful. The empirical examples deconstruct the common narrative that Republicans are always in favor of “administration light” while Democrats are the ones who impose burdens on citizens. Anticipating ideological criticism on this assessment, Herd and Moynihan affirm, “our observations about the politics of burdens are not intended to score a partisan point but to correct an existing misconception about how partisanship relates to burdens” (p. 245). Embedding their approach in a critical theory, for example by borrowing from Lyotard’s (1984) notion of the end of grand narratives, could have further legitimized this intention. Certainly, this book has much to offer for scholars and practitioners alike. Readers of the Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory will be interested in the book because it introduces a new perspective on bureaucratic rules in citizen–state interactions. This topic has received inadequate attention in the public management literature. Herd and Moynihan provide an analytic framework for the assessment of administrative burdens that will surely elicit future investigations in the fields of public administration and public policy. The compelling case studies include concrete recommendations that can inform practitioners who are involved in US policy and in search for levers to make bureaucratic encounters less onerous. Herd and Moynihan’s call for a government that better serves its citizens should not die unheard of.

t: It Depends on What You Share: The Elusive Cost Savings from Service Sharing
abs: Intermunicipal cooperation is the most prevalent alternative service delivery method for US local governments. While aspirations for budgetary savings are one motivating factor, increased service quality and regional coordination are also important goals. We use an original 2013 survey of local governments in New York State to assess the level of service sharing and outcomes. We match our survey with 20 years (1996–2016) of service-level costs data to explore the relationships between sharing and costs across 12 common local government services. We contribute to the literature by providing the first multivariate assessment of the effect of cooperation on costs in the United States, and we contribute theoretical insights on the objectives and type of cooperation to explain differences in the effects of cooperation on costs across a variety of services. Our multivariate time series regressions find that service sharing leads to cost reductions in solid waste management, roads and highways, police, library, and sewer services; no difference in costs for economic development, ambulance/EMS, fire, water, and youth recreation; and higher costs in elder services, and planning and zoning. These differences are explained by whether services have characteristics such as asset specificity and the ability to achieve economies of scale on the one hand, or if sharing leads to greater administrative intensity or promotes other objectives such as quality and regional coordination outcomes on the other hand. We also analyze the effect of sharing on service costs over time, and find solid waste, roads and highways, police, and library are the only services where costs show a continued downward trend. These results show the limited role for economies of scale, even in asset specific services. Because cost savings are elusive, public sector reformers should be careful not to assume cost savings from sharing. The theoretical foundations for service sharing extend beyond economies of scale and transaction costs. Scholars should give more attention to organizational form and the broader goals of sharing.

t: Socioeconomic Representation: Expanding the Theory of Representative Bureaucracy
abs: To date, representative bureaucracy scholarship has primarily focused on the potential for increased racial/ethnic and gender representation in the public-sector workforce to improve outcomes for minority and female clients. However, the potential for socioeconomic representation to benefit those from a lower socioeconomic background has not been thoroughly explored. Using the Early Childhood Longitudinal Study—Kindergarten Cohort 2011 and a student fixed-effects approach, I begin to fill this gap in the literature by investigating whether socioeconomic representation—above and beyond and intersecting with racial and ethnic representation—affects teachers' perceptions of their relationships with students. Heterogeneity by an organizational context likely to affect the saliency of SES is also explored. Overall results show no evidence that SES match between teachers and students influences teachers' rating of relationship quality with students. For low-SES black students, racial representation persists as an important factor in better teacher–student relationships, even controlling for socioeconomic representation. However, for low-SES white students in contexts where SES is likely to be particularly salient, socioeconomic representation has a significant positive effect on teacher–student relationship quality. Results exploring the interaction of racial and socioeconomic representation are also presented. Finally, theoretical and practical implications, as well as directions for future research, are discussed.

t: Procedural Fairness and the Legitimacy of Agency Rulemaking
abs: We examine the relationship between procedural fairness and the legitimacy of rulemaking decisions made by government agencies. Evidence from a survey experiment indicates that the perceived fairness of the rulemaking process is closely tied to procedures designed to make it more transparent and to encourage greater citizen participation. However, our findings do not indicate that fair procedures bestow unconditional legitimacy on agency rulemaking actions. Rather, they suggest that the effect of procedural fairness is context-dependent and complex, with legitimacy perceptions varying across policy domains and being driven by the institutional avoidance of procedural controls rather than the procedures themselves. Thus, there may be significant limitations on the ability of fair procedures to impart legitimacy to bureaucratic policymaking.

t: How Government Agencies React to Termination Threats
abs: Much research following Kaufman’s classic study Are Government Organizations Immortal? has investigated the claim that government agencies enjoy great security and long life. Less attention has been paid to Kaufman’s thesis that government agencies facing a termination threat have strong incentives to react. In a study of the on-going Norwegian local government amalgamation reform, we demonstrate that this type of government agency reacts by hoarding (i.e., a last-minute flurry of spending) when faced with a termination threat. This finding shows that agencies facing termination threats are active players in the termination game. We discuss implications for research on agency termination and design implications for reformers of the public sector.

t: Relational Mechanisms in Complex Contracting: Factors Associated with Private Managers’ Satisfaction with and Commitment to the Contract Relationship
abs: The complexity of human service delivery means that contracts are often incomplete or contingent. When contracted services or products are complex, relational contracting can function as a critical informal accountability mechanism. This study introduces and tests a conceptual framework of relational processes and organizational factors hypothesized to inform private human service contract outcomes. Data from a 2015 survey of private nonprofit and for-profit human service organizations in five counties are used to examine factors associated with two proximal indicators of success in human service contracting: commitment to and satisfaction with the contract relationship. Findings provide support for our conceptual framework, highlight the multidimensional nature of trust and commitment, and identify key differences in the relational processes associated with commitment and satisfaction to the contract relationship. Communication quality, trust, and flexibility were associated with satisfaction, whereas interdependence, flexibility, and asset specificity were associated with longer-term commitment to the contract relationship. For-profit ownership was associated with lower commitment and satisfaction. Implications for research and practice are discussed.
