t: Supervisory Leadership at the Frontlines: Street-Level Discretion, Supervisor Influence, and Street-Level Bureaucrats’ Attitude Towards Clients
abs: Steering street-level bureaucrats is utterly complex due to their discretion and professional status which grant them relative autonomy from supervisory directives. Drawing from transformational leadership theory, this article explores the opportunities these work conditions provide for supervisory leadership at the frontlines. Looking at street-level bureaucrats’ attitude towards clients, we analyze how the frontline supervisor affects this core perception that protrudes the human judgments street-level bureaucrats are required to pass in their use of their discretion. Using a survey dataset of 971 street-level bureaucrats and their 203 frontline supervisors, this study shows that frontline supervisors function as an attitudinal role model to street-level bureaucrats. Moreover, their supportive leadership behaviors are crucial to them upholding a positive attitude towards clients. Supportive leadership does not unequivocally strengthen the supervisor’s position as an attitudinal referent, though. These findings challenge pessimistic assessments of the potential for supervisory leadership at the frontlines. Theoretical and practical implications are discussed.

t: Municipal Government Form and Budget Outcomes: Political Responsiveness, Bureaucratic Insulation, and the Budgetary Solvency of Cities
abs: One of the fundamental questions in democratic governance is whether policies are best decided by elected officials or by appointed bureaucrat-experts. The study examines this issue in the context of how municipal government form influences government-wide budgetary solvency. Government form creates distinct incentives for executive action that shape budget outcomes. In mayor–council governments, the elected executive’s desire to be reelected increases responsiveness to voters’ preferences. Vote maximization incentivizes the adoption of policies that are popular among voters but can lead to budgetary imbalance. In contrast, the appointed executive in the council–manager form is interested in career advancement, which she achieves by building a reputation for leading a fiscally sound government. Insulated from the demands of voters, the manager can rely on expert knowledge and professional norms to choose policies that result in balanced budgets. Using data from audited financial reports for 655 mid-sized and large city governments in the United States from fiscal years 2006 to 2013, the econometric analysis shows that council–manager cities have stronger budgetary solvency compared with mayor–council cities.

t: Don’t Tase Me, Bro
abs: Discretion is endemic to bureaucracy; bureaucrats exercise discretion millions of times per day, and some of those instances lead to abuse. Although Steven Koven notes in the preface “one should not tar all agencies with the broad brush of dangerous overreach” (p. vi), the focus of the book is on the dark side of discretion with emphasis on the substantive areas of law enforcement and foreign policy using examples from the United States. Koven’s approach is broad ranging and seeks to tie his topic to the big questions in public administration and political theory. He begins with a well written chapter linking discretion to the classical theories of public administration discussing Wilson, Weber, Taylor, Faoyle, and Gulick. While one might quibble with some omissions (Frank Goodnow, Leonard White, Paul Appleby) and wish that the citations were to the original work rather than secondary sources, this is an excellent introduction. Chapter 2 moves to political theory and considers discretion and democratic accountability all the way back to Plato and Aristotle. Chapter 3 brings the focus back to bureaucracy with a discussion of various checks on bureaucracy starting with the Friedrich-Finer debate; the chapter is a nice review of the literature and would be a good starting place for a PhD student seeking a summary of the literature.

t: Integrating Immigrants into Local Communities
abs: Immigration into the United States has emerged as a critical issue in the 21st century. Current US immigration policy is largely based on the 1965 Immigration Act, and immigration policy has not been altered through comprehensive immigration reform since 1996. The lack of federal policies that adequately and effectively address the changes in immigration since the 20th century have resulted in multiple ad hoc executive orders across presidential administrations. While the media largely focuses on the national level, concerned with these executive orders and judicial responses, contemporary scholars have begun to examine the effect of this immigration policy vacuum on state and local policy and administration, particularly in seeking to understand the role of restrictive policies at the state or local level. Newton (2018) argues that the dispersion of responsibility for immigration, with state legislatures creating immigration policy, may produce more contentious immigration politics, and Heinrich (2018) argues that state and local levels are increasingly using discretionary administration to fill the gaps left in federal policy. In Welcoming New Americans, Williamson adds significantly to the discourse on local government immigration administration by emphasizing the key role local government response plays in aiding or hindering immigrant incorporation into a given community. She challenges scholars to examine how accommodating responses can best assist both immigrants in exceling in the community and established residents in accepting immigrant presence. Local governments are responsible for addressing immigrants in their communities and therefore are at the forefront of immigration administration. How cities choose to respond to the immigrants in their communities dramatically impacts the lived experiences of immigrants and the community as a whole. Williamson brings needed insight to understanding when local governments act to accommodate immigrants and how interactions with and engagement of immigrants takes place. To accomplish this, Welcoming New Americans is divided into three sections: describing local government responses, explaining which circumstances are likely to generate a particular response, and evaluating the consequences of immigrant accommodation. Williamson uses a mixed methods approach, drawing her results from an in-depth case study analysis of four cities across the United States and a national survey of local government officials. Through a thorough analysis of these data, Welcoming New Americans illustrates that local governments are more likely to accommodate immigrants than apply restrictive policies, higher-level issue framing and implementation are critical to local government responses, and accommodating policies do not necessarily result in immigrant incorporation. Williamson begins by summarizing local government responses between 1990 and 2015 in four new immigrant destinations: Elgin, Illinois; Yakima, Washington; Lewiston, Maine; and Wausau, Wisconsin. All are small to medium sized cities that were chosen based on their significant shift in ethnic makeup. Elgin and Yakima are recipients of Latino immigrant populations; by 2015, 45% of residents in both Elgin and Yakima were of Latin American origin. Williamson finds that despite moments of restrictive behavior, Elgin government leaders attempted to accommodate immigrants. City officials hold meetings in Spanish, and the city sponsors Latino organizations and cultural celebrations. However, growing national anti-immigrant rhetoric since 2006 has limited immigrant accommodation efforts in Elgin. In contrast, Yakima officials did not act to address their growing immigrant community. Leaders chose to ignore federal mandates, which created restrictive outcomes. For example, the failure to adhere to the Voting Rights Act regarding the translation of voting materials and bilingual polling staff created a restrictive environment for Spanish speakers. However, in 2006 new city leaders began to accommodate immigrants more, actively engaging with their sister city in Mexico and treating the Hispanic Chamber of Conference and Greater Yakima Chamber of Commerce equally in budget decisions. However, leaders in Yakima continued to grapple with accommodating its large Mexican American population. Lewiston and Wausau are recipients of refugee populations. In 2001, Somalis began arriving in Lewiston. Initially city leaders complied with federally mandated services for refugees; over time this compliance evolved into active accommodation. Lewiston maintains a city welcoming proclamation, whereby all are explicitly “welcomed, accepted, and appreciated” (p. 38). In 2017, the city council acknowledged the role of Somali entrepreneurs in city development and the role they will continue to play in the future of Lewiston. In comparison, Wausau began receiving Hmong refugees in 1976. Williamson demonstrates that Wausau follows a similar trajectory to Lewiston that extends from compliance to accommodation. However, local government officials did not initially take on an accommodation perspective; instead local nonprofits and foundations led the way, stimulating active accommodation from the city. To ensure that her findings were more generalizable, Williamson chose to survey government leaders in a random sample of 503 small to midsize cities where immigrants reside. Of the 503 cities surveyed, 598 leaders in 373 cities across 46 states responded. The results from the quantitative analysis confirmed her case study results. She finds that inaction often characterizes municipal responses. However, local government inaction is not neutral; instead it often results in restriction or accommodation. How and on what issues local governments choose not to respond have consequences for the experiences of immigrants in the community and for how established residents view immigrants. Contrary to the media and scholarly focus on restrictions at all levels of government, Williamson finds that substantial accommodation exists at the local government level while restriction is atypical. Both sets of data confirm that local governments are more likely to accommodate than restrict immigrants in their communities. This accommodating nature corresponds with the argument in Raadschelders et al. (2019) that government responses at the local level are largely palliative in nature as it is the local government’s responsibility to address the day-to-day realities of immigrant presence in a community. Williamson examines a number of issues around responses and the reasons for these responses. Framing of worthiness is particularly salient in such responses. Newton (2005) argues that immigrants are vulnerable to elite framing of deservedness. Policies at the federal level, along with partisan politics, affect the framing of communication about foreign-born residents. Whether foreign-born residents are framed as immigrants or as refugees appears to affect local government response. Accommodation varied across the four case studies, but the refugee-receiving cities of Lewiston and Wausau were more welcoming than Elgin and Yakima, implying a greater impression of perceived deservedness of refugees as compared to Latino immigrants. The framing of immigrants as illegal aliens may have affected local government responses in Elgin and Yakima, while the framing of refugees as clients appears to have affected the perceived deservedness of refugees in Lewiston and Wausau. However, the data are not so clear-cut. Cities were found to be more likely to respond to immigrants when the immigrants in a community are perceived to be of Hispanic origin and poor. The distinction then arises in how many immigrants of a particular framing must be present to render an accommodating local government response. Cities who reported “a small but visible refugee population” were associated with an 11% increase in accommodating practices (p.111). Previous research demonstrates that a growing ethnic minority is connected to feelings of threat among residents, but Williamson argues that this threat does not translate to the creation of more restrictive policies by local government. Although the data do not support the literature regarding how ethnic threat shapes local policies, the type of migration, which in turn is associated with a susceptibility to framing whereby refugees are conceived of as clients of local services and immigrants as lawbreakers, may support types of threat. In fact, cities located near federal border enforcement where the framing of lawbreakers is more striking were associated with a 4% decline in the accommodating index. Scholars should take up where Williamson left off to examine how this distinction in migration framing affects local government response. This is a particularly relevant line of inquiry, as refugees are often framed as a potential threat or security risk. This current framing is more negative than earlier framings of refugees. Williamson further demonstrates that bureaucrats’ and elected officials’ attitudes toward immigrant accommodation may be less distinct than previous literature illustrated. Bureaucrats and elected officials tend to see immigrant incorporation through an economic development lens, and, as such, tend to support immigrant accommodation. This finding is contrary to bureaucratic incorporation theory that argues that bureaucrats are more likely to accommodate than elected officials. Part of this variation may be due to the variables examined—Williamson uses official’s stated attitude rather than policies enacted by local government—but nonetheless provides an important demarcation. Of interest are the perceptions of police officials who are more likely to view the importance of gaining immigrants’ trust but are less likely to view immigrant presence positively. Framing continues to affect local officials’ attitudes, as increased immigrant enforcement tasks have been delegated to the local level, which may affect how police officials view or define immigrant communities. Moreover, accommodating policies do not necessarily equate to immigrant incorporation. Such policies can result in tensions within the community as established residents do not have the same incentives as government officials to accommodate immigrants, and may view immigrants as outsiders. Accommodation can create strong ties between immigrants and city elites but may not assist in truly incorporating the immigrant community in a holistic manner. Williamson highlights the importance of “creating opportunities for meaningful interethnic contact that makes positive understandings of immigrants more resonant” (pp. 273–74). Her call for further research to understand which policies can foster immigrant incorporation and community acceptance is particularly critical for communities increasingly facing these issues across the United States today. While Williamson addresses the connection between national and state policies on the local level perception of immigration, much more work in this area is required. Further analysis on how state policies affect municipal welcomeness would be useful to better understand the links across government levels and public opinion at the local level. How do state level policies affect municipal workers’ perceptions? What state level policies are more likely to affect the way in which local governments accommodate or restrict immigrant integration? How can states assist local governments in creating better outcomes for immigrants and established residents? Overall, Williamson’s theoretical model of municipal response places municipalities on a continuum from active restriction to active accommodation and can be quite helpful to scholars seeking to understand the implications of immigration policy making. Welcoming New Americans addresses a significant gap in the literature and brings to light the need to examine the overarching role of immigration governance in a federalist system, particularly immigration policy implementation, the impacts of policy, and how to create better outcomes for immigrants and established residents of communities.

t: Policy Sectors and Professions: The Institutional Foundations of Activist Public Health Policy
abs: In many countries, health systems have developed impressive levels of medical care and organizational complexity, providing treatment of a broad range of conditions for the vast majority of citizens and arresting the attention of academic observers, politicians, and the general public. But the health care system has an older step-sister that is much less in the public eye, much poorer both in resources and reputation, and more often concerned with lackluster tasks such as hygiene, immunization, or telling people to clean their teeth or cut back on drinking and smoking. It is to Philipp Trein’s credit that he calls our attention to public health, the older step-sister of clinical medicine and presents this study of the development and relationship between the two, pointing out the significant difference between individualistic, curative health care and collectivist, population-oriented public health. In times of new threats by infectious diseases such as Ebola or the Measles, increasing incidence of multiple drug resistance, and growing prevalence of chronic disease, this is a timely and laudable contribution. Trein’s book is also commendable for its emphasis on the interdependence—coevolution, as Trein calls it—of the two sectors. The book considers this coevolution in an internationally comparative perspective, combining the detailed substantive focus of public policy analysis with the broader generalizations of Historical Institutionalist comparative politics scholarship. Trein is also right in highlighting the great diversity in institutional design of the two health sectors and their relationship across countries—this last point being not so surprising, as this usually emanates from such internationally comparative undertakings. Public health and health care systems, Trein argues, are two policy sectors that evolve in partially interdependent and partially autonomous ways; they coevolve. The form of this coevolution is interesting, because it is consequential for the extent to which activist public health policies are feasible. Coevolution of the two sectors, Trein argues, takes the form of four different institutional and policy-related types, which he calls types of sectoral coupling. The types reflect different kinds of institutionalization of the two sectors, their interaction, and the extent to which there is cooperation and policy integration (i.e., shared policy agendas and jointly developed policies) between the two. Two institutional and behavioral dimensions define the types. First, institutional distinctiveness of the two sectors pertains to the question of whether they are organizationally autonomous or integrated; second, responsiveness pertains to the behavior of professionals in the two sectors and the question of whether they talk to each other and coordinate their work. Tight coupling refers to a situation in which the two sectors are highly responsive and organizationally highly integrated. Under conditions of loose coupling, the two sectors are institutionally distinct but their actors are still responsive and work together. Noncoupling describes organizationally integrated policy sectors in which professionals concerned with the tasks of public health or curative medicine do not work together, and a decoupled setting is one in which we find neither organizational integration nor responsiveness (complete separation). The four types are consequential because only the responsive types are able to produce integrated policies, combining the agendas and resources of both sectors. The book’s explanation of the four types of coevolution draws on the two dimensions of the typology, with sectoral distinctiveness and autonomy being a facet of power sharing in the political system at large, such that integration of the two public health sectors is to be found in countries with unified government. Mutual responsiveness of professions working in the two sectors is a function of the institutionalization and, as the author claims, the strength of those professions. Where professions are strong and politically active and position themselves in competitive, pluralist systems of interest group institutionalization, Trein expects to find responsiveness, whereas “weak” professions in corporatist systems of interest mediation produce situations with little responsiveness between policy sectors. Since unification of government structures and professional interest organization are both institutional variables and, as such, better suited as intervening factors than as independent variables, the author introduces contextual factors such as problem pressure, fiscal strain, and the notion of political environments that are generally amenable to policy integration and responsiveness to account for institutional change and policy development. The case studies examined in the book exemplify the four types, with the three Anglo-Saxon countries (Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States) representing the responsive types while Switzerland and Germany are constellations with little responsiveness and interaction between professionals of the public health and the health care systems. The book’s empirical chapters present evidence from the histories of health policy over the course of the past 150 years. The case studies trace institutional integration or differentiation as well as responsiveness and cooperation of the professions working in the two policy sectors in four time periods. Trein puts much effort into presenting the historical material very systematically, in each chapter highlighting how it relates to the conceptual framework and in the concluding chapter summarizing the different pathways of coevolution very clearly (cf. p. 240). He is also very explicit about points in which theoretical expectations were not met by the historical record. This analysis demonstrates the author’s strong commitment to reconciling the detailed historiographic work of public policy analysis and policy history with the explanatory and generalizing ambitions of comparative politics scholarship. The reader is never lost in the complexity of historical detail; there is no ambiguity, and the author succeeds in lucidly and transparently identifying distinct cross-national patterns of coevolution as well as explanations for those patterns. It is this very clarity that also exposes limitations of the conceptual framework and some weak spots in the explanation and the historical analysis, however. Here, I would first make some remarks about the conceptualization of the dependent variable, coevolution, and then comment on the explanation of the patterns of coevolution both with regard to its theoretical underpinnings and the historical evidence presented in support of this explanation. The book’s central theoretical claim is that public health and curative medicine coevolve, that is, they are interdependent yet potentially distinct. Coevolution occurs at the intersection of two dimensions, organizational distinctiveness of the two sectors and responsiveness of the professional staff working in the two sectors. This results in the four types of coupling of health care and public health described above. The first of the two dimensions, organizational distinctiveness, is systematically underdeveloped, however. This holds with regard to the empirical case studies, where the author often reports that his findings about the organizational dimension were not in line with his theoretical expectations. It also holds with regard to theoretical underpinnings, where the meaning of “unified government,” conceptually the main explanation of institutional integration of the two policy sectors, remains unclear. Chapter 3 of the book, which discusses the institutionalist underpinnings of the two central hypotheses about responsiveness and distinctiveness, presents a whole bundle of theorizing on government unification or fragmentation, ranging from arguments from the comparative federalism literature to veto player analysis. These arguments are mobilized to motivate the author’s expectation that distinctive and autonomous sectors are to be found in polities with dispersed political power. This is conceptually imprecise, as it does not specify where and in what way political power is dispersed (in legislation, in state structures, in administrative resources, in patterns of political mobilization and interest organization, etc.), and why and how this should have an impact on administrative structures in policy fields. It is not fruitful theoretically, for instance, to use a blanket characterization of German government as “relatively unified” (p. 169) if the intention is to explain details in authority patterns and administrative structures of public health and health care. The German polity may be politically relatively centralized and unified, but public administration is not unified but decentralized. In terms of political power, German corporatism and German federalism are among the core institutions that have been explicitly designed to render the German state “semi-sovereign.” Therefore, while conceiving of sectoral distinctiveness as a facet of power sharing in the political system at large is an interesting approach, it would require more theoretical work specifying precisely how we can establish a connection between dispersed or concentrated executive authority and the organization of tasks in policy sectors. In addition to the fact that the explanation of the distinctiveness dimension is not fully developed, the overall status and significance of that dimension are not entirely clear. It seems of lesser interest than responsiveness, as responsive types of coevolution, whether loosely or tightly coupled, are the constellations in which policy integration, cooperation in public health campaigns, and overall reform activism on public health are more likely. Throughout the book there is an underlying notion of “successful public health activism,” capturing the evolution of public health out of its subordinate status and the “creation of a global public health strategy” (p. 250). This is an interesting and important prospect, and asking when and under what conditions it may occur is certainly a valid and highly significant question. But this question remains implicit and is never accurately formulated as a research question; it is never properly theorized, and it is an entirely different question than what identifying types of coevolution between two policy sectors can answer. Therefore, if successful institutionalization of activist public health is the core commitment, and if cooperation and responsiveness of professionals working in public health and the health care systems is the principal explanation, then the core conceptual tool should reflect this. A typology is probably not the most suitable approach for studying stages of development toward an integrated and activist public health policy because we would then not be talking about a typological distinction but, instead, about an ordinal scale of more or less successful public health efforts. If the underlying core commitment is explaining the success of the public health effort, an outcome of professions’ responsiveness, and responsiveness, in turn, is a function of the “strength” of professionalism, then a few words about that causal connection are in order. In the kind of semantic shorthand-fashion that sometimes makes reading this book more cumbersome than necessary, Trein often refers to the “responsiveness of the two sectors.” As only actors and not sectors can respond or cooperate, he means the extent to which professionals working in the two sectors are willing or able to cooperate across sectoral boundaries or within settings in which sectoral boundaries have become unimportant or nonexistent. Responsiveness, according to Trein, is a function of the political strength of professions. In the case of public health and health care, this includes primarily the strength of the medical profession and its interest organizations. In pluralist systems of interest organization in which interest groups and professions compete based on their political appeals, professional organizations mobilize on a broader substantive agenda; they are willing to respond to the commitments and agendas of adjacent policy fields, such as public health. In corporatist social insurance systems, by contrast, there is no need for broader political mobilization; professional representation accords public status to organized interests, and professions focus on their narrow material interests. Therefore, weak professionalism renders policy sectors nonresponsive and, as a result, less able to produce integrated policy solutions. The first difficulty of this argument is that we learn a lot about the political strength or weakness of the medical profession, but the image of the public health profession (or professions?) remains pale. So, it is a one-legged cooperation, responsiveness to an unknown interlocutor. The argument’s main problem, though, is rooted in the theoretical underpinnings of the notion of “weak professionalism” as core building block of the explanation of coevolution types. As in the case of organizational distinctiveness and unified government, this notion is based on a somewhat selective and skewed reading of large theoretical literatures on systems of interest mediation. In the central point, namely the assessment of a profession’s (or an interest group’s—Trein never decides which) strength, it runs flatly against core findings of these relevant literatures, especially when it comes to assessments of corporatism. While there is no divine verdict against disagreement with core claims of a literature, some discussion would have been required. This is what is often lacking here—there is no recognition and discussion of Mancur Olson’s seminal argument that interest groups under pluralist conditions may be more prone to defending narrow interests and more powerful in doing so but are especially ill-suited for taking on more encompassing views, which are more likely in corporatist systems of interest organization with their broad peak organizations (Olson 1982: 47–50). The book includes no acknowledgement of Peter Katzenstein’s groundbreaking argument about a state (Germany’s state), rendered semisovereign, precisely because of this political system’s entrenched corporatist structures in which a strong and centralized civil society organizes policy sectors such as health with some degree of autonomy, thus constraining the central government’s interventionist prowess (Katzenstein 1987, especially pp. 23–34). This idea may explain sectoral distinctiveness, but Trein does not use this opportunity and instead sets out to contend that organized medicine is politically weak in corporatism. There is no appreciation of scores of writings about veto-group politics in health policy making, in which the strength of organized medicine may have made cost-containment a cumbersome task in many health systems but has not per se undermined the activist policy making or quality of health services in either the health care or the public health domain. Finally, not much actual evidence is provided for the claim that lesser amounts of actual interaction, cooperation, and responsiveness amount to lesser efforts and success in sanitation, vaccination campaigns, health surveillance, health education, or however one might circumscribe the substantive scope of activist public health policy. The conceptual weakness, again, spills over into the cogency of the empirical narratives. For instance, it is a bold assertion (to put it mildly) to call organized medicine in Germany politically weak. This profession has been able to determine prices for medical services (i.e., their income) practically unilaterally for decades, which is not much of a sign of political weakness. To write a 30-page policy history of public health in Germany, a narrative that amounts to an image of institutional underdevelopment of that sector because of the putative political weakness of health professions, without ever mentioning the names of Robert Koch, Emil Bering, Paul Ehrlich, Rudolf Virchow, all of whom are towering figures in the history of public health, amounts to a bold assertion, to say the least. It is also testimony to the difficulties of a style of argument as predominantly institutional and structural as this one. Organizational distinctiveness is a function of government fragmentation, an institutional variable. Responsiveness is a function of professions’ political strength and status, likewise primarily a function of the professions’ institutionalization. Schematically applied, this leaves little room for understanding the actual policy histories, and that, in turn, leaves us wondering how much explanatory power this account of coevolution has at the end of the day. This book is full of interesting ideas and observations. The way in which they are put together into a conceptual argument, however, is not fully convincing. There are (too many) weak spots on the conceptual and theoretical level, and readings of underlying theoretical literatures are somewhat thin and skewed at times. As a result, some of the empirical narratives—likewise often lacking the historical and policy field-related depth and detail that would be necessary to sustain this argument—do not capture key developments in the countries and in the time periods under review. As such, the five-way comparison does not successfully substantiate this book’s explanation of coevolving policy sectors. It is the very commitment to clear-cut hypotheses and systematic inquiry that has brought forth the limitations of the argument. But then, social science is a collective undertaking, one might say, and much can be said in favor of putting an interesting and novel set of observations and possible relationships on the table, leaving much room for improvement. We read our colleagues’ work as much in search of inspiration and creative disagreement as we look for instruction and conclusive results. In that spirit I can say, do read this book! But do not believe what you read.

t: Can Government Public Communications Elicit Undue Trust? Exploring the Interaction between Symbols and Substantive Information in Communications
abs: Effective public communications have been proposed as a remedy for citizens’ distrust in government. Recent studies pointed to the emotional effect of symbolic elements, entangled in government public communications (e.g., logos, images, and celebrities). Still, they did not examine the interaction between these symbols and the substantive information in communications about bureaucracies’ performance and policies. Exploring this interaction is important for understanding the theoretical mechanisms underlying the effect of symbolic communication on citizens’ trust. Also, it is essential to assess symbols’ potency to unduly compensate for unfavorable or logically unpersuasive information, and enable public organizations to escape justified public criticism. Building on the social psychology Elaboration Likelihood Model, I theorize that symbols may increase citizens’ trust by conducing citizens to pay less attention to logically unpersuasive information, and thus offsetting its negative effect. I test this indirect mechanism via a large survey experiment, focusing on the Israeli Environment Protection Ministry. The experimental results support the research hypotheses and suggest that the effect of symbolic elements is stronger when communications include logically unpersuasive information. I discuss the implications of these findings for democratic responsiveness and accountability.

t: The Political Psychology of Citizen Satisfaction: Does Functional Responsibility Matter?
abs: The provision of public services is a key responsibility of elected politicians. Research suggests that citizens’ satisfaction evaluations of public services are incomplete representations of service quality and performance. However, little attention has been given to the political nature of service evaluations. Based on the theory of (partisan) motivated reasoning and the literature on responsibility attribution, we argue that citizens provide more favorable evaluations of municipal services when the responsibility for these services is vested in political principals with matching partisanship. Drawing on original data from a two-wave pre-post panel survey of Danish voters in the 2017 municipal elections, we employ a difference-in-differences estimator to identify the effect of a partisan match between voters and elected municipal leaders on citizen satisfaction with municipal services. We furthermore nest a survey experiment in the panel survey to test whether partisan bias in citizen satisfaction emerges when the line of functional responsibility between political principals and public services is clear and not dispersed across multiple actors. Our findings provide support for the hypothesis of partisan bias in satisfaction evaluations. We further demonstrate the importance of clarity of responsibility; partisan bias seems to come into being when the functional responsibility of municipal leaders for public services is clear and not dispersed across multiple actors, pointing toward a possible mechanism of partisan bias in citizen satisfaction.

t: From Maximizing to Minimizing: A National Study of State Bureaucrats and Their Budget Preferences
abs: Since the 1960s, public choice theorists have stigmatized bureaucrats as budget maximizers who only care for expanding their own agencies. Despite evidence revealing much more diverse budget behaviors, scholars have almost exclusively focused on studying budget maximizing and its associated factors. To address this limitation, this study employs a multi-level cross-classified logistic regression model to explore factors associated with budget-minimizing preferences or goals instead. While budget preferences may differ from actual budget requests, where administrators may ask for higher or lower funding, they are the initial goals for strategic budgetary requests and deserve attention. Using four decades of the American State Administrators Project (1974–2008), we analyzed responses from eight surveys reflecting the views of approximately 9,500 state agency administrators across all years. We found a notable number of state administrators holding no aspirations for agency or state budget expansion—budget minimizers. As is the case when administrators formulate their actual strategic budget requests, agency heads’ ultimate goals are shaped by not only the characteristics and internal attitudes of administrators but also by the entire context in which agency heads are embedded. Governors, clientele groups, state budgeting rules, and the fiscal environment all played a role when state administrators formed minimizing budget preferences. Interestingly, while some of these actors continually helped shape budget minimizing over time, others had more limited or time-bound effects.

t: Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory Police as Emergency Responders: Organizational or Personal Resilience?
abs: Public administration’s scholarship regarding police departments and officers has been an important avenue for understanding representative bureaucracy and street-level bureaucracy theories, as well as other topics related to organizational and individual behavior. This has provided important information regarding bureaucratic and organizational decision making, but studies typically focus on the everyday activities of police departments and officers. In Policing After Disasters: Stress, Resilience, and the Challenges of Emergency Management, Terri M. Adams and Leigh R. Anderson focus on the role that police officers play as first responders in natural disasters. The authors do this by examining qualitative and quantitative data collected directly from police officers after three incidents: Hurricane Katrina, 2005, in New Orleans, LA, and Gulfport, MS; the 2011 Tornado Super Outbreak in Tuscaloosa, AL; and the 2010 earthquake and tsunami in Santiago and Constituciòn, Chile. The lofty goal of the book is to use a wealth of data from police officers responding to these three incidents to answer a series of research questions regarding organizational structures and culture as well as individual officer activities, behavioral responses, disaster and role induced stress, and coping mechanisms. The book contributes not only to our understanding of how police departments respond to disasters at the organizational level but also considers how organizational variables may interact with extreme events to affect the behavior of police officers in unexpected ways. The findings in the book may have application for other emergency services administration organizations, such as fire departments, emergency medical services, and, to some extent, emergency call centers. For public administration scholars, the book has the potential to be an interesting examination of how organizations and street-level bureaucrats bend and adapt in stressful situations. The authors focus on natural disasters, which is a choice they do not spend a lot of time explaining. It is important to note because we know more about officer reactions and activities in response to man-made events and terror attacks than natural disasters, where attention is often on other types of first responders, such as firefighters, aid workers and nonprofits, and national organizations, such as the Federal Emergency Management Agency. The focus on policing in natural disasters is an important contribution of this book to a number of fields, including criminal justice, sociology, public administration, and emergency management. The authors examine the effect of natural disasters at both the organizational and individual levels. At the organizational level, the authors do an excellent job of explaining the role of police departments and officers pre- and postdisaster, including their role in the preparedness stage of a disaster situation. Police are often thought of primarily as first responders and security after a disaster, but the authors point out the important work that officers performed before each of the disasters examined in the book. Officers engaged in warning the community and organizing evacuation activities as well as preparing departments for impacts from the disaster through mitigation activities. These activities differed by department and disaster type, as different disasters have different warning periods (hurricanes provide longer periods than tornadoes and earthquakes), which significantly impact the ability to make short-term preparations in the community and the organization. It is important to understand this difference to fully grasp what police do before a disaster as well as how a disaster will affect the police department itself. The authors also do an admirable job exploring the effect that a disaster has directly on the police department, both physically (i.e., damage to organizational infrastructure) and to organizational behavior and operations. Public administration theories often examine the role of culture in organizational performance, management, and survival. Likewise, this book focuses on how organizational culture present predisaster can help or hinder a department and officers following a disaster. Key takeaways from the book include the need for flexibility and a culture that supports officer well-being throughout the disaster cycle, especially during recovery. At the individual level, the authors focus on the role a disaster plays in the ability of officers to complete their duties and serve the community. Much of what we know about stress, depression, and post-traumatic stress disorder in emergency responders has developed out of the psychology literature. The authors use this research to examine how the unique stresses that accompany a disaster affect the ability of officers to perform as first responders. This is best represented in Chapter 3, where the authors discuss role conflict and role strain in the context of Hurricane Katrina and the Chile earthquake and tsunami. As the authors note, previous research finds that officers do not typically suffer from role conflict when engaged in emergency management after a natural disaster; however, these two disasters affected very large geographic areas which meant that many of the responding officers and their families experienced direct damage from the event. In the case of these two extraordinary disasters, officers were much more likely to identify role conflict between obligations to work and family than in disasters that had a smaller geographic scale and therefore may not directly affect as many officers. This suggests that there is not a one-size-fits-all understanding of how first responders will react to a disaster. Instead, we need to understand the scope of a disaster and its potential direct effects on officers before we can understand how an officer will perform in the response and recovery phases of the disaster cycle. The above example is also a good illustration of how comparing departments across countries and organizational structures can provide insight into approaches for overcoming some of the personal hardships of disaster response, including role conflict. In the Chilean system, the government has programs in place to attend to the needs of officers’ family members following a disaster. The authors discuss how beneficial this was in helping officers overcome role conflict, which may make officers less likely to engage in behavior that is detrimental to the response effort, such as leaving their post to attend to their family and property. The authors collected data from multiple, diverse police departments preparing and responding to three different types of disasters, but the majority of the book is dedicated to Hurricane Katrina and the New Orleans Police Department in particular. While the authors acknowledge this in the introduction, it becomes, perhaps, the biggest weakness of the book. In particular, when discussing maladaptation (Chapter 4) and misconduct (Chapter 5), the authors focus wholly on the New Orleans Police Department. There are reasons to believe that maladaptation was unique in New Orleans due to the fact that the damage from the Hurricane was so widespread that it affected most officers and their families. This led to a greater likelihood of officers leaving their post to attend to private matters, either temporarily or permanently. Likewise, New Orleans was distinct in the study of misconduct because of a longstanding culture of corruption in the police department, which was likely exacerbated by the unique nature of the disaster. The authors miss an opportunity here to understand these phenomena in a broader, more common emergency management context. The authors end the book with lessons learned and suggestions for improved disaster resilience for police officers. Most of the findings in the concluding chapter have been discussed in previous and ongoing research in the fields of public administration, psychology, sociology, and disaster science. The authors mention the necessity for responding organizations to be flexible in order to overcome unexpected loss of communication or damage to facilities and infrastructure. This is further evidence for the ongoing debate in the emergency management literature about the structure of emergency response, including Incident Command Systems, and the ability of systems to be flexible in the face of expanding disasters. While the lessons learned and suggestions made are helpful, few of them are novel approaches. The conclusions regarding the effects of disaster response on individual officers, including mental health and physical loss, focus primarily on what the police department can do to prepare officers for the tasks involved with disaster response. Some of the suggestions are specific, such as providing basic needs during and after a disaster, so that officers do not have the added stress of trying to obtain these resources. The authors extend this to the officers’ families in order to remove some of the role conflict experienced by officers (as illustrated by the New Orleans case). While the publishers market this book toward sociology, criminology, labor studies, public policy, and the environment (via the back matter), this book would also be appropriate for public administration programs in which there is either a certificate for or focus on emergency management, homeland security, or emergency services administration. It is important to note that a foundational understanding of the phases of emergency management is probably important as they are mentioned in the book but not described. The book itself is clearly designed and marketed for education purposes, as each chapter nicely concludes with key takeaways and discussion questions. The discussion questions are a good mix of knowledge, application, and evaluation, which is a nice resource for instructors and should lead students to a better understanding of the material. Instructors should consider this text as it applies to understanding the phenomena of police as first responders in natural disasters and as a supplemental course reading. This text would not be a good supplement for a research methods or design class. The authors discuss their data collection in the introduction to the text, and they have an impressive amount of data through interviews, focus groups, and surveys with police officers after each incident. However, it is not always apparent throughout the book which data source is used or how the data are analyzed, and in some instances (e.g., Chapter 4), the authors deviate from their own data description to examine other source material. The authors focus less on rigorous data analysis and more on presenting the information in a way that is accessible to both academics and practitioners. In conclusion, the role of police as first responders in emergency management is sometimes misunderstood, and the effect of disaster response on police departments and officers is understudied. Adams and Anderson provide a rich picture of the role of police as first responders in a disaster context. However, their primary focus on Hurricane Katrina, despite data collection in three different disaster and organizational contexts, limits the generalizability of their findings. Hurricane Katrina is an exceptional case given the scale of the disaster and the organizational context of the New Orleans Police Department. It is hard to generalize the experiences of these officers, in particular their maladaptive and sometimes criminal behavior, to other disaster contexts. Hopefully, the authors work will lead to further studies in the natural disaster context to provide richer data sources for understanding police departments and officers as first responders.

t: Pension Reforms and Public Sector Turnover
abs: Over the past decade, many states have reformed their retirement systems by reducing benefit generosity, tightening retirement provisions, introducing non-defined-benefit (DB) plan options and even replacing DB plans with defined-contribution plans. Many of these reforms have affected post-employment benefits that public workers will receive when they retire. Have these reforms also affected the attractiveness of public sector employment? To answer this question, we use state-level data from 2002 to 2015 and examine the relationship between state pension reforms and public employee turnover following the reforms. We find that employee responsiveness to the reforms was tangible and that it differed by reform type and worker education. These results are important because the design of public retirement benefits will continue to influence the ability of the public sector to recruit and retain high-quality workforce.

t: Adopting Integrative Governance in the Midst of Democratic Uncertainty
abs: A citizen is one who helps to realize [and make] the purpose for which this nation exists. (Follet 1930) Margaret Stout and Jeannine Love’s latest book Integrative Governance—Generating Sustainable Responses to Global Crisis seeks an answer to how public administrative governance practices can bend toward individuals working, thinking, and learning together about social and environmental issues. The book consists of three parts addressing why integrated governance should be used, what integrative governance is, and a call for integrative governance over current practices of administration. The authors begin with a soft critique of collaborative governance literature before explicitly dispelling the current assumptive and philosophical fundamentals of collaboration as misaligned with what it actually takes to forge new ideas and novel understandings of complex social issues. Stout and Love argue that the failure of collaborative governance is evidenced by an overwhelming amount of time and resources spent coordinating institutional sectors and not enough attention to the type of relationship building needed to achieve a collaborative advantage if the intent is to nurture direct democracy. As a result, existing collaborative efforts regress to forms of domination or compromise rather than integration (a la Mary Parker Follet); these forms aren’t much different than what society experiences with representative government and bureaucracies and their associated hierarchies. Throughout the book, Stout and Love never stray too far from their concerns with current forms of collaborative governance as being less mindful about (1) individuals coming to situations with different and unique interpretations of the world that pre-shape meaning, which therefore (2) necessitate that governance practices be intentional about processes of engagement while de-centering authority by (3) creating mechanisms for access, openness, and acceptance of the other when (4) forging new relationships that are essential for increased understanding and inspiring new ways of thinking and making space for ground level solutions to vexing social challenges.

t: Giving Time: Examining Sector Differences in Volunteering Intensity
abs: Sector differences in prosocial motivations and behaviors among workers receives a great deal of attention in public administration scholarship. Extant literature consistently finds public sector workers are more likely to engage in prosocial behaviors, such as volunteering, than their peers in the private sector. Less attention has been paid to the sector gap in volunteerism along the intensive margin. Using time-diary data, which accounts for potential social desirability bias, from a nationally representative sample, this study investigates the gap between public sector workers and their private sector counterparts. The results suggest that public sector workers spend more time, on an average day, volunteering than observably similar private sector peers, and the difference cannot be explained by other observable differences between public and private sector workers. The gap in volunteer intensity is largest at the local level and among teachers. The implications of these results for research and practice are discussed.

t: The Life and Times of a Boundary Spanner
abs: Over recent years, the world of public management and governance has evolved in response to the changing nature and challenges presented by modern societies. The most significant of these include a torrent of complex and cross-boundary “wicked” issues and problems that single organizations and actors cannot resolve by managing autonomously; ever-increasing demands from service users and the wider public for meaningful involvement in shaping and evaluating public services; constant pressure to design and deliver efficient and effective services against a background of limited resources; and, a realization that the needs of future generations must be embraced to achieve a sustainable future. This world is shaped and defined by a scaffolding of a myriad number of boundaries, including organizational, professional, social, cultural, and psychological. Some of these boundaries are real and others socially constructed. They are dynamic and shifting; they can form barriers of variable permeability or conversely help to facilitate interactions; and, they interweave together to form complex policy spaces. Consequently, contemporary public management and governance necessitate the effective management of these boundaries in the course of the pursuit of public policy objectives. This can be achieved partly through structural interventions and policies designed to facilitate and ease cross-boundary management, but, more critically, occur through the management practices and actions of public actors—the boundary spanners with their boundary-spanning behaviors. The literature on this particular cadre of public actors is comparatively silent, so the work by van Meerkerk and Edelenbos in Boundary Spanners in Public Management and Governance is especially welcome. Clearly, public organizations no longer have the luxury, capacity, or discretion to operate independently within a highly interconnected governance framework, and boundary spanning has become a core activity of contemporary public management. And who best to navigate a course through the turbulent waters of complex contemporary public organizations and governments but the boundary spanners? Actors equipped and experienced with the skills and competencies to manage, weave, and bridge the myriad of boundaries that constitute modern public management and governance structures and processes. This book is the product of a systematic literature review designed to provide a comprehensive and interdisciplinary synopsis and analysis of the topic. The authors’ stated intention is to provide an overview of the state of the art on boundary spanners and boundary spanning, paying particular attention to the theoretical underpinnings of the topic, and to advance research on the subject within the context of public management and governance. The book opens by identifying and discussing the drivers and imperatives for boundary spanning behavior—the complexity of policy issues and problems; fragmentation and functional differentiation; and, the increasing pressure for participation and co-production by public service users and citizens. The analysis is drawn toward the many different and shifting types of boundary produced by such a system, and the logical demands for boundary spanners to manage and govern in this environment. This constitutes a compelling set of arguments, that needs tempering only by a note of caution around the danger of perceiving all public problems and issues as complex and interdependent when arguably some remain best treated more independently through conventional management practices. The book moves on to consider the theoretical roots and evolution of boundary spanning theory, drawing on a range of interdisciplinary literatures. Such an approach adds considerable richness to the analysis but, inevitably, enhances contestability. It explores and compares three main perspectives—structuralist, role, and action—and from these distills a definition of a boundary spanner. Defining who exactly might be classed as a boundary spanner is far from straightforward. The authors opt for a broad definition that stresses four main components of the role—relational, coordination, mediation, and entrepreneurship. This is intended to identify boundary spanners by their behaviors and activities rather than their formal role in an organizational hierarchy. Consequently, this definition envelopes a potentially large number of actors at different levels of the hierarchy, tasked with different activities and devoting different proportions of their work time to boundary spanning. Questions might be asked as to whether a senior manager and a frontline practitioner, for instance, can be included in the same group, or whether a different classification is necessary. Also, is the definition sufficiently robust and nuanced to apply to boundary spanning actors in the public, private, and third sectors? Or might context make a material difference? On the question of detecting boundary spanners and their behaviors, the book reviews the research methodologies employed for that purpose. It reveals an equal balance between quantitative and qualitative approaches—each with their respective advantages and disadvantages—and distinguishes three different ways: by specific organizational role or function, by the frequency of the cross-boundary interaction, and by specific activities. It concludes by drawing attention to the dearth of case study, mixed method and longitudinal approaches in the study of this topic. Certainly, these approaches potentially offer the prospect of a greater understanding of the working lives of boundary spanners, and of reflecting the dynamic, complex, contextualized, nuanced and ambiguous nature of their boundary-spanning behaviors and practices. In terms of what the research suggests boundary spanners do, the book identifies four main profiles—fixer, bridger, broker, and innovator/entrepreneur. The nature and challenges inherent in each of these roles are considered in detail, but although the “interactivity” between them is recognized, and this is a criticism of the literature, not the authors, there is little discussion of how and when these roles are deployed in various permutations to best effect. It is interesting to know whether a single boundary spanner needs to acquire proficiency in all these roles, or whether different boundary spanners, with different boundary spanning role specialisms, need to be assembled to manage particular challenges. A discussion of the antecedents of boundary spanning behavior is found midway in the book. Arguably, it might have been considered earlier, in conjunction with a clearer exposition of the structure-agency debate*** that must frame any exploration or the role of boundary spanners and their behaviors. Nevertheless, the authors detect four main factors that impact boundary spanning behavior—individual determinants that relate to the competencies and capacities of individual actors; environmental characteristics that define structure; role definition and stressors; and, organizational support and feedback. These factors are used to construct an integral framework of antecedents of boundary spanning behavior. This suggests a complex set of relationships representing more of a tentative research framework rather than a prescriptive analysis of the direction, sequence, combination, and valence of individual factors and relationships. There is certainly no shortage of hypotheses for potential researchers to investigate in the future. A key, but highly challenging question, concerns what impact boundary spanners have through their boundary-spanning behaviors. Unsurprisingly, the reviewed literature on this subject was limited, but as one might expect, could be categorized broadly into personal impacts on the boundary spanners themselves; those influencing the performance of their employing organizations; and interorganizational outcomes relating to partnerships and alliances of various types, as well as an enhancement of relational capital in a particular geographical area or network, and a contribution to a general discussion of structural factors relating to integration and organizational/resource/sectoral alignment. But, the sad state is that very little research has been undertaken on these different impacts, and there is a clear case for studies designed to measure the performance of boundary spanners and their management in contemporary public management and governance. A clear justification for the promotion and nurturing of boundary spanners is overdue. In some areas, the book might have offered some additional insights and exploration. For instance, some reflection on, and comparison of boundary spanning management with other forms and practices of public service management would have been of great interest. What are the comparisons and contrast between them? Do public managers have to switch between different management approaches when tacking different challenges and are different skills and competencies needed? The challenges associated with managing the respective demands of multiple accountabilities are an important area of investigation, and more in-depth exploration is needed into the balance between a boundary spanners’ grasp of core knowledge and content on a particular policy area, and their relational and processual skills. The book is relatively silent on the leadership role of boundary spanners, an omission that future contributors in this field of study need to address. Leadership is an activity that is relevant at different levels in the organizational hierarchy, and the nature of boundary spanning management impacts on leadership styles, approaches, and practices. In terms of theoretical insights, the contribution of boundary object theory is one that offers considerable potential in this area of study. Lastly, the education, training, and development of boundary spanners are other areas that might have received greater attention, particularly for the benefit of policymakers and practitioners. If cross-boundary management is a core management activity of the future, there is a pressing need to ensure that public managers are appropriately trained and equipped in the necessary skills and competencies. Although this book is considered suitable for a range of audiences, its primary appeal is likely to be academics, researchers, and students. There are clear lessons for policy and practice in this area, a number of which have been identified, but public managers and practitioners tend to be drawn to more prescriptive material in the form of toolbooks, practice guides, and key lessons to guide their practice, and may perhaps find the evidence somewhat too theoretical and academic for their needs. But be under no illusion, this is essential reading for all those interested in understanding the nature, role and behaviors of this important actor in the collaborative spaces of public management and governance, now and into the future. It is a well-written, structured and comprehensive systematic review on the subject, and represents the most up-to-date exploration of boundary spanners and their behaviors. In particular, it offers a rich research agenda for future academics and students.

t: The Tacit Dimension of Public Sector Attraction in Multi-Incentive Settings
abs: The public sector provides a broad range of incentives to apply for jobs, but these incentives have rarely been studied in concert. The present study disentangles how job candidates form intentions to apply for a public sector job in multi-incentive settings and how this process depends on public service motivation (PSM). Using a speeded categorization task in an experimental vignette methodology with 340 current job seekers in the United Kingdom, we focus on perceptions that potential applicants have, or do not have, of a range of employment attributes (i.e., extrinsic, intrinsic, and prosocial) when they screen job advertisements. Results of multilevel analyses suggest that perceptions of intrinsic and extrinsic attributes are similarly strong predictors of the intent to apply for public sector jobs, whereas perceptions of prosocial employment attributes do not yield such an overall effect. However, PSM moderates the relationship between perceptions of prosocial attributes and application intentions, but only among nonstudents. Theoretical implications for the alignment of PSM with extrinsic rewards are discussed. Findings are also important for human resource managers in the public sector who want to adjust their recruitment strategies to specific target groups.

t: Absenteeism in the Public and the Private Sector: Does the Public Sector Attract High Absence Employees?
abs: Evidence from many countries shows that public sector employees have considerably higher rates of absenteeism than have private sector employees. Based on regression analyses of a large probability sample of the Norwegian population, this article shows that most of the sector difference in long-term absence can be accounted for by taking into consideration the sociodemographic characteristics of the workforce and the occupational composition in the two sectors. A clear sector difference in short-term absenteeism cannot be accounted for in this way. A direct effect of the working or employment conditions in the two sectors is also not a likely explanation, since workers who switch between the sectors are not more absent when they are in the public than when they are in the private sector. Thus, the high level of short-term absenteeism in the public sector seems to be due to a selection of absence-prone individuals to the sector. Since motivational factors are likely to be relatively more important for short-term than for long-term, these findings indicate that lower work attendance motivation in public sector employees may be the main driver. These patterns are consistent with an economic explanation in which people with low attendance motivation select to the public sector, since the work attendance incentives are weaker there. The degree to which the results are compatible with the theory public service motivation is also discussed.

t: Bureaucratic Representation and the Rejection Hypothesis: A Longitudinal Study of the European Commission’s Staff Composition (1980–2013)
abs: This article analyzes the evolution of the staff composition of the European Commission from 1980 to 2013 using the theory of representative bureaucracy. The article first demonstrates how the Commission formulates guidelines which aim at offering fair levels of representation to each member state. However, comparing recruitment targets and actual staffing figures reveals very heterogeneous staff levels. Some member states enjoy unexpectedly high levels of representation whereas others present very low levels. The latter are particularly intriguing and open the door to the formulation of a “rejection hypothesis.” This hypothesis challenges one of the foundations of the theory of representative bureaucracy and leads us to suggest that the theory be enhanced in order to take into account its context of implementation in terms of consolidated or contested statehood, which in turn may explain the phenomena of rejected offers of bureaucratic representation.

t: The Effect of Shared Service Centers on Administrative Intensity in English Local Government: A Longitudinal Evaluation
abs: “Administrative intensity” (AI) describes the proportion of total resources that organizations spend on administrative support functions rather than primary service and production processes. We test whether “sharing” administrative activities between organizations leads to a fall in AI due to economies of scale, as is often supposed, using organizational and financial data from more than 300 English local authorities. We employ multi-wave change score regression analysis to relate changes in AI from 2008 to 2016 to levels of shared services participation, and further test whether reform performance varies by category of local authority, type of administration, or degree of structural complexity. Although we find that some measures of AI fell slightly over this period, this was unrelated to shared service adoption for any category of local authority. Sharing of clerical rather than professional types of administration, and sharing by organizations and within partnerships characterized by lower structural complexity, also failed to improve reform outcomes. Faulty assumptions about the extent of administrative scale diseconomies in English local government partly explain this significant reform underperformance.

t: Reducing Minority Discrimination at the Front Line—Combined Survey and Field Experimental Evidence
abs: Despite laws of universalistic treatment, bureaucrats have been shown to discriminate against minorities. A crucial question for public administration is how bureaucracies can be organized in ways that minimize illegitimate discrimination. Especially, since theories suggest that prejudices happen unintentionally and particularly under high workload, bureaucrats’ working conditions may be important. Four randomized experiments support the notion that bureaucrats discriminate as a way of coping with high workload. Most notably, a field experiment randomly assigned teachers to reduced workloads by giving them resources to have more time with the same group of students. In a subsequent survey experiment—using a fictitious future scenario unrelated to the resources provided in the field experiment—discrimination was minimized in the field treatment group, but persisted in the control group. The results thereby support the notion that even though discrimination among bureaucrats does not (only) occur in a reflective manner it can be reduced by altering the way bureaucrats’ work is organized.

t: Mix and Match: How Contractual and Relational Conditions Are Combined in Successful Public–Private Partnerships
abs: In explaining public–private partnership (PPP) performance, both contractual and relational conditions play a role. Research has shown that these conditions may complement each other in successful PPPs. However, which specific combinations of conditions and how these combinations may influence PPP performance remains unclear. Building on the ideas of neo-institutional economics, principal–agent theory, relational contracting, and governance theories, this article explores the mix and match of contractual aspects and relational characteristics in successful PPP projects. A fuzzy set qualitative comparative analysis (QCA) of 25 PPP projects in the Netherlands and Flanders (Belgium) was used to test how contractual factors, such as the use of sanctions and risk allocation, and relational conditions, such as trust and conflict management, jointly shape the performance of PPPs. The results show three different combinations of conditions that match with high performing PPPs. These configurations often consist of a mix of contractual and relational conditions, which confirms our initial expectation that these factors complement each other, but a combination of only relational conditions is also present.

t: Organizational Dissolutions in the Public Sector: An Empirical Analysis of Municipal Utility Water Districts
abs: The proliferation of special-purpose districts and the increasing complexity of local governance systems has been well documented. However, even as new special districts are created, others are being dissolved. This article investigates the extent to which both internal and external factors are at play in municipal utility district dissolutions. Decades of existing empirical studies on private, nonprofit, and interest organizations show that factors internal to organizations, such as institutional structure and resources are significant covariates of organizational mortality. Equally important are external factors, where density dependence and resource partitioning pressures influence organizational survival. Public sector organizations, such as special-purpose water districts, operate in relatively well monitored and statutorily constrained environments, however. Drawing upon the organizational mortality literature, we examine when and why municipal utility water districts that operate in fragmented service delivery systems dissolve. The results show that the relationship between internal and external organizational variables and special-purpose organizational dissolutions is more nuanced than existing research suggests.
